#102305. Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2571 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.
  • Sources indicate that today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy?
  • A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

Sources indicate that today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Industry observers note that the main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

Recent findings suggest that leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

There are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data highlights him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

Photo: National Geographic Archives.

Industry observers note that his article, cryptically titled Among the Big Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

It has been revealed that much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”.

Sources indicate that A recent study revealed that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

There is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper says that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

Recent findings suggest that there is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

Photo: National Geographic Archive.

Sources indicate that his previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

Recent findings suggest that in a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

He continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

In a recent development, it would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

Industry observers note that amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Sources indicate that clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

According to recent reports, as soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

According to recent reports, A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

Recent findings suggest that the review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”.

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”.

Recent findings suggest that A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind.

If he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

According to recent reports, in his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

Chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind.

The other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

The three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

Later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

In a recent development, clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949.

What exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

He had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which showed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

Sources indicate that clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

If I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how significant they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

Industry observers note that his 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

Industry observers note that clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

Industry observers note that in fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally said the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”.

On Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East.

Recent findings suggest that it is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

One history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

It has been revealed that as I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

Recent findings suggest that the area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Industry observers note that the line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary New Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”.

The real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he demonstrates to the world.”.

‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer.
  • Recent findings suggest that “We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life.
  • Industry observers note that it was clear this was the season to try to kill him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer. They kept tabs on the buck with trail cameras and debated when it was time to shoot the high and wide whitetail.

Recent findings suggest that “We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life. “Over last summer when he was still in velvet we saw on cameras that his rack had completely blown up and got huge, with lots of palmation.”.

Industry observers note that it was clear this was the season to try to kill him. The brothers hunted hard during a 23-day stint in October, with one of them in a stand every day.

Sources indicate that “I was just the lucky one sitting that day when the buck slipped up,” says Zack, a business-studies student at Louisiana Tech University. “My brother, dad, and I put in a lot of work hunting that buck. I would not have taken this deer without their help.”.

The Halberts had multiple setups around their 80-acre hunting property. Zack took the buck from a ground blind on a 48-degree morning in late October.

It has been revealed that “The blind faced the woods, and I’m looking one way out a window, then leaned the other way, and there he was at 21 yards,” Zack indicates. “It’s crazy how you can go from calm and in two seconds go into full panic mode.”.

Sources indicate that zack watched the buck for three long minutes as he waited for a broadside shot. When the buck finally turned, he drew and held at full draw for about 15 seconds. Then he let fly.

The buck took off, and Zack watched where it disappeared into the woods. Then he called his brother, dad, and girlfriend with the news.

In a recent development, “When I shot I was so pumped I almost shook the ground blind over. Before I got out of the blind I was trying to stop shaking enough to finish my prayer for what a blessing it was.”.

Zack began trailing the deer into timber, but the blood became faint and he decided it would be best to call in a tracking dog.

“I didn’t want to mess up on this deer,” he says.

Tracker Eric Perry and his dog, Blue, arrived that evening.

“It was getting toward dusk when the dog got there and was put on the buck’s trail,” Zack claims. “Blue found it in just 15 minutes. The arrow was a good hit, but there was no exit hole and so not a good blood trail.”.

In a recent development, the deer had died in a creek, and Zack had to wade into the cold water to get his buck out. The crew dragged the deer out of the timber and loaded it into a truck and headed home. Zack estimates it was 5½ years old, and Buckmasters scorer Chris Bates measured Zack’s buck at 205 3/8 inches.

In a recent development, although Buckmasters has a different scoring system than the one used by Boone and Crockett and Pope and Young Clubs (and therefore scores aren’t apples-to-apples), it’s worth noting that the largest nontypical killed with a bow in the state scored, according to P&Y records, 206 5/8 inches. That deer was taken in January 2012 by Alton McLead.

“I know my grandpa Dan, who isn’t with us anymore,” indicates Zack, “wouldn’t have believed his eyes if he got to see this deer.”.

#102303. Breaking: Bear Tracks All Over the Arizona Trail

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2897 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Bear Tracks All Over the Arizona Trail

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this morning we woke up bright and early at our tent site right beside the trail.
  • By the time the sun came up this morning we had already been walking for a while.
  • According to recent reports, the views this morning were unbelievable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this morning we woke up bright and early at our tent site right beside the trail. I was really hoping that we were going to get surprised last night by Leaf at some point, but she never did wind up catching up to us. At least today she’ll be heading into town from a trailhead less than 20 miles from where we were camped. So, she isn’t too far from a road, a town, and some hiking friends. I made coffee this morning pretty early and then laid in my tent for a while. Then the two of us got packed up and were walking on the trail before the sun was up. There isn’t too much awaiting us along the trail up ahead. Today we will be going past that major trailhead and highway crossing about 19 miles into the day. But other than that, it is just going to be us and the trail for the next few days. Depending on how far we go today and tomorrow, we’ll hopefully be able to head into town the following evening to resupply and recharge.

A small bear track in the muddy red clay.

By the time the sun came up this morning we had already been walking for a while. And the trail actually had some fun surprises for us. Thanks to all of the rain, the trail had been covered in mud for the last couple of days. Which meant that any animal that hiked through the area would leave deep footprints in the trail. We got to follow the path of a bear which had been walking through this area in the last couple of days. It left behind such clear footprints in the red clay mud. It was cool to see the larger prints left behind by its back feet. This section of the trail was beautiful all on its own, but the prints in the mud added something special to it all.

According to recent reports, the views this morning were unbelievable. After all of the rain the red clay has the most incredible, deep color to it. And all of the trees and plants are vibrant and lush.

For the first hour or two of the day the trail was a dark red clay, complimented quite well by the lush pine trees and other shrubs surrounding the trail. The rising sun lit up the rocky mountainside off in the distance and made the red clay glow. That was a stunning way to start off the morning. We had some gradual climbing to do and continued to see bear prints along the trail on and off. If I was a bear, I would also love to follow the trail. It is a perfect path through the wilderness! It’s also one reason why some hikers prefer to set up their camp a little way off the trail at night. In the night, the trail is an animal highway through the woods. You never know what you’ll see if you follow a trail through the dark.

Industry observers note that I liked the way that the layer of clouds off in the distance was resting right above the mountain range. The Arizona Trail sure had a lot of trees today!

In a recent development, lucky for us, the mud wasn’t too bad this morning. Most of the moisture had been sucked in to the earth already. Leaving behind only the deep, saturated color that the water left behind. These sections of red clay are some of my favorites here in Arizona. The color looks incredible right beside the deep greens that we are able to enjoy thanks to all of the rain. I’ve had a lot of people reach out to say that the red clay typically doesn’t look nearly as vibrant as it does right now. All of the rain makes the color all the deeper, which I’m quite thankful for.

One particular stretch of trail that walked along a large red rock hillside.

It has been revealed that over the course of the morning the trail was following along a large cluster of rocks off in the distance. Some of them were shaped like tall, jagged chimneys. I really enjoyed the view as we got even closer to the rocks, before eventually the trail veered off. We actually ran into some people on the trail today as well. There are a ton of road crossings and trailhead throughout this area. One guy was out doing some trail maintenance scouting. I’m sure that the individuals doing trail maintenance through this area have their work cut out for them with all of the rain and flash flooding. An entire section of trail can so easily get washed away if enough water pours through an area. We’ve been lucky so far with the state of the trail. But there have definitely been a lot of sections and areas with fresh rock fall.

Sources indicate that clouds starting to roll in off in the distance. I thought we were going to get poured on! But as we stood on top of a ridge, we could see the storm blowing off and away from us.

It has been revealed that by the late morning the temperature dropped a bit, and some dark clouds began to roll in. I hadn’t seen any rain in the forecast, but it certainly seemed like we had some coming for us. We stopped on top of a hill for a quick break, and each put our rain gear on while we watched it pour down off in the distance. It made me think about Leaf behind us, and all of our friends up ahead of us. The storm managed to skirt right on by us, and it hardly rained more than a sprinkle. But we could tell that someone somewhere was getting rained on. It felt nice to keep the rain gear on as we continued along, at least for a little while. We watched as the bulk of the storm blew by us and the skies got bright and blue off in the distance up ahead.

Recent findings suggest that for a mile or two the trail slowly approached this cluster of unique rocks. A couple of them look like stone pillars.

It has been revealed that as we got closer to the trailhead and highway crossing, we did wind up getting rained on a bit. Which was surprising because the rain started just as the skies turned blue! It was only a sprinkle though. I used my sun umbrella to stay dry and the rain passed swiftly. Though, even just a light rain caused the mud on the trail to build back up again. I’m just hoping that the mud won’t be too bad for the rest of the day. Prior to reaching the trailhead, we ran into a couple more day hikers and one person on horseback with another horse being pulled behind them. The second horse had the cutest little pink saddle on. Then it wasn’t long until we reached the trailhead as well.

These bright yellow wildflowers have been growing all along the trail.

Arizona Trail signs near the trailhead about 20 miles into our day.

For some reason it always feels exciting to pass by a trailhead, even if you aren’t heading into town. Perhaps it’s the possibility of receiving some trail magic there or having something else eventful occur. When we actually passed by the trailhead though there was hardly anyone around and we just continued along. And we only made it another mile or two before we encountered the next obstacle ahead of us. There was another deep river crossing for us to ford! This one was quite easy in comparison to our river crossing yesterday. We walked around to see if there was any way that we could avoid getting our feet wet, but there was not. So, we both plunged in and got our shoes and socks soaked. Then sat on the other side of the river to enjoy a lunch break.

After Slide and I crossed the river, we sat here in the grass to eat lunch.

Industry observers note that the sky was still dark off in the distance and it certainly felt like it was going to rain at some point. Both of us figured this would be a good time to stop and eat, just in case the rain did start up. I had packed out one of those tasty bite tikka masala meals which I enjoyed there. Those always do a great job of filling me up. Then I cleaned out my socks and shoes and debated on whether or not I should put my rain gear back on. We were going to begin going uphill, so I knew I was going to get super-hot in rain gear. But if it’s windy at all then I still get wet when I’m using just my umbrella. I decided to opt against it and just figured that if the rain did start and was heavy, I could just stop and put my rain jacket on later.

Sources indicate that in the early evening the trail briefly followed along this massive slab of rock. It reminded me of sections of the Appalachian Trail in New York.

Recent findings suggest that the rain wound up holding off as we continued along. It sprinkled on us briefly but didn’t persist. Once we left the river, we did have a bit of climbing to do. Then we were up on top of the nearby hill and just continued along up there. In some places the trail itself was just a massive boulder beneath the ground. We had some open and exposed views, and the weather was nice and cool. It felt like we had gotten pretty lucky already for the day. It wouldn’t be long before I had to get my feet wet again in yet another small stream crossing. I probably could have tried harder and kept my feet dry, but it felt like a lot of work. I also always have the strong memory in my mind of slipping on a rock in a river crossing in Northern California on the PCT and breaking 2 of my fingers last year. All to avoid getting my feet wet! I actually wound up getting more wet than I would have if I just crossed through the river normally, because I slipped and fell. Of course, at the time I didn’t realize that I’d broken 2 of my fingers. But 4 months later I still couldn’t apply any pressure to the two fingers on my right hand, so it feels like a safe assumption now.

Recent findings suggest that A photo that Slide took of me when we were on top of this ridge. The trail stayed up there for the rest of the evening and the views just got better and better.

According to recent reports, as we continued along the trail was pretty rocky, but in exchange we were graced with some great views. The trail went through some areas with vibrant foliage as well. The leaves were a perfect spectrum of light greens, yellows, oranges, and deep reds. It reminds me so much of hiking in Colorado this time of year. We even saw a bunch more bear prints along the trail over the course of the evening. And some prints that appeared to be a large dog. They definitely didn’t look like mountain lion prints, in my opinion. I’m not sure what else they could be besides a dog!

I figured these were just big dog prints, but I still like the way that they looked in the mud.

According to recent reports, by the time that the sun began to set we were up top of a ridge and would be continuing along it for the rest of the evening. The sun cast an incredible glow across the wheat grass and other plants surrounding the trail. There were loads of bright yellow wildflowers and prickly pear cacti throughout the area as well. It was a really beautiful way to end off the day. Sometime after 5PM we passed my favorite bear prints of the entire day. There were some prints which were incredibly deep and had standing water inside of them. It just really highlighted how massive the prints were. I wonder where this bear was going, and if it was the same bear whose prints we saw earlier on in the day. I’m sure it’s not, but bears can travel very far in a day if they want to.

Perfectly defined bear prints right on the trail.

In the early evening, we entered into the Mazatzal Wilderness in the Tonto National Forest. At this point the sun was just starting to go down, and the sky was putting on quite the show for us. The trail got much rockier in this section and there were way more cacti lining the trail as well. The timing wasn’t great, because we would be looking for camping sometime soon. When the trail is lined in rocks and cacti it can be hard to find a place to set up your tent. As we walked, I snacked on some pistachios and enjoyed the views. We were in the perfect place to be able to enjoy the sunset this evening.

The sun was beginning to set, and we were in the perfect place to enjoy it.

In a recent development, the trail stayed pretty much the same for the rest of the night. There were rocks all over the place and a ton of cacti. Camping options seemed limited at best, if not nonexistent. But we just kept our eyes peeled for any area with less rocks and some flat ground. Just after it got dark, we did wind up finding an area just off the trail which didn’t seem too bad. It was a little rocky and lumpy but was definitely much better than what we had been seeing. It was hard to imagine that we would find anything much better than this anytime soon. So, we decided to just call it a day then and there. We both got our tents set up, and it was a great feeling to take off my shoes and socks. They weren’t soaked, but they definitely weren’t dry. The worst part about wet shoes and socks, in opinion, is putting them back on the next morning. Especially when it is cold out! It could take my breath away.

Enjoying that last bit of light before the sun completely dipped behind the mountains off in the distance.

In a recent development, once my tent was up, I got comfortable inside and ate something. Then did my stretching routine before calling it a night. We made it 31 miles today which was pretty good. Sure, we could have gone a bit further to make our life easier tomorrow and the next day. But we certainly didn’t need to. I think we’ll wind up having another early start tomorrow morning which will make up for it. There is a ton of elevation gain tomorrow, so I’m curious to see how that goes.

If you enjoyed this blog and would like to support my hike by buying me a soda or a snack along the way, there is a “Tip the Author” button below! It links directly to my Venmo. Any and all support is incredibly appreciated!

The tall wheatgrass looked almost pink under the glow of those cotton candy clouds.

This was easily one of the best views that I’ve had the pleasure of enjoying thus far on the Arizona Trail. The sunsets and sunrises out here have been fantastic.

According to recent reports, how does a person really get in to thru hiking ? My question isn’t so much about physical prep or gear prep but more in regards to the actual timeline and logistics of planning the adventure? #102300. The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1386 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1386 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • In a recent development, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent new route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

In a recent development, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman remarked. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two upcoming routes with Blake Berghoff.

Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

It has been revealed that bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he remarked.

According to recent reports, he explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, substantial storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

The unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

In a recent development, “[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

One unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman indicates this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Industry observers note that approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

“Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

“Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

Recent findings suggest that asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

It has been revealed that the base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

Recent findings suggest that at the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

According to recent reports, that attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment challenges, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he mentioned.

According to recent reports, in the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

“However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he noted. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

Industry observers note that heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

The summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Sources indicate that however, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

In a recent development, route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

The trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to new terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman said.

They then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

Descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The new 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

Alaska Considers ‘Unprecedented’ Closure of Public Land to Hunting, Trapping Along Controversial Ambler Road

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road.
  • While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat complications, the recent development is creating even more consternation.
  • According to recent reports, “It’s unprecedented,” notes Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road. The decision would be part of a push by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority to build a road creating private access to a future mining district focused on copper and zinc deposits.

While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat complications, the recent development is creating even more consternation.

According to recent reports, “It’s unprecedented,” notes Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers. “We’re supposed to allow for balanced use of all of our resources. This would show preference to one resource over another.”.

Sources indicate that the proposal, which the Alaska Board of Game will consider during an online meeting Friday, would close 1 mile on either side of the 211-mile proposed road in northern Alaska to all hunting and trapping. It first became public in February and is part of a memorandum of understanding between several Alaskan native corporations and the state. The proposed closure is part of a “subsistence safeguard,” according to a story in the Alaska Beacon. Subsistence hunters could still cross through the road corridor to access other legal hunting grounds.

Industry observers note that the hunting and trapping ban would begin July 1, 2029, and remain in place through at least Jan. 1, 2036, regardless of when or even if the road is built, Glaves claims.

The Board of Game considered formalizing the MOU in a July meeting, and opposition was fierce, says Glaves. Still, many Alaskan organizations could not prepare comment because the meeting was in the middle of fishing season. As a result, the board tabled the discussion until its formal meeting in January.

Industry observers note that A few months later, the Alaska Fish and Game commissioner revealed another special meeting Nov. 20 to discuss the project, allowing only written public comment and no oral testimony.

“That isn’t illegal,” Glaves says, “but it’s not in the best interest of engaging the public.”.

Even more importantly, if the closure passes, it tells Alaskans that state public land can be shut down to access at the request of an anticipated industry and with no stated biological need.

Recent findings suggest that the road has not been built, and there’s some question about whether or not Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the Democratic governor-elect, will support the project. He has not stated a position publicly but has remarked he will carefully evaluate money spent by the state. The Industrial Development and Export Authority, an economic development arm of the state, would be responsible for building the road. The Alaska Wilderness League, which opposes the project, estimates it could cost the state more than $2 billion including construction, maintenance, and financing.

The preemptive nature of the closure is particularly troubling to conservation groups.

Read Next: The Ambler Road Project Would Jeopardize One of the Last Great Wilderness Hunts in America.

Recent findings suggest that “There is no compelling reason to establish these restrictions years before the project is constructed or in the absence of demonstrated need,” she wrote on Nov. 4. “Doing so would also set a troubling precedent of using the Board’s time and public resources to evaluate hypothetical impacts of projects that may never materialize, rather than addressing actual wildlife management and public access concerns as they arise.”.

#102296. Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1071 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • Recent findings suggest that crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

Recent findings suggest that crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an key figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up looks for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

It has been revealed that as the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

According to recent reports, though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

Industry observers note that some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

According to recent reports, the caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

Sources indicate that the depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

The main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

It has been revealed that attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

Recent findings suggest that the high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and Latest Mexico.

Industry observers note that the few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

Recent findings suggest that despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” indicates Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

The columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

It has been revealed that essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

According to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

As for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

In a recent development, the arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

Industry observers note that in terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

There have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

In a recent development, “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

On a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Recent findings suggest that “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

Vasiliev remarked that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Sources indicate that baia says the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no latest soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

#102290. Breaking: Why am I’m Hiking?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1300 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Why am I’m Hiking?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • So, the question I usually get from people when I tell them I’m hiking the Appalachian Trail is, “Why?”.
  • There’s a lot of emotion behind that question, and it can lead to very different answers.
  • I could talk about the people who ask with frustration, disbelief, sadness, or even fear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So, the question I usually get from people when I tell them I’m hiking the Appalachian Trail is, “Why?”.

There’s a lot of emotion behind that question, and it can lead to very different answers.

I could talk about the people who ask with frustration, disbelief, sadness, or even fear. Maybe they’re worried that the things I normally handle will now fall into their laps. Then there are the people who sound surprised or curious. I may have to explain exactly what backpacking is and what thru-hiking entails. Those conversations lead to a whole different brand of questions. These are the best discussions, and I can go down all kinds of rabbit holes about gear, food, concerns about animals, and where I’m going to sleep.

It has been revealed that the question, though, is still this: Why am I going to hike for six months, leaving a perfectly good couch, bed, wife, career, and a couple of affectionate cats behind? All to be cold, wet, and worn out most days from doing nothing but walking? Miles and miles of walking.

Sources indicate that I have to go way back, maybe 14 years ago, when my wife and I were exposing the kids to all kinds of different vacations, ideally the kind that didn’t cost much. For several years, we had been camping at National Parks, enjoying the sights and activities. One of those years, when we were in the Rockies, we saw a young couple leaving camp with their tiny kids, each carrying an even tinier backpack. We remembered a couple of backpacking trips we’d taken after we got married but before we had kids. The gear had been sitting on a shelf for years, but at least we still had some.

“Let’s take the kids next year!”.

The next year, we suited up. Our kids now had their own tiny packs. We had food, fuel, and ponchos in case it rained.

Did I mention we were on a small section of the Appalachian Trail in the Smoky Mountains?

It rained for three days straight before we even started our hike, and then it rained for the three days we were on the trail. Thankfully, we stayed in shelters, but there were a lot of lessons learned. Lessons about food, clothing, footwear, water treatment and yes, raingear. Still, I came off the trail with a huge smile. Can’t say that about the kids, but for me, I had a blast! Spoiler – both my kids are now young adults and camp, sometimes willingly but I’m getting distracted.

The biggest lesson for me came when we got off the trail. My daughter pointed to the large sign behind me that remarked “Appalachian Trail” which told me about its more than 2,150 miles of hiking that people tackle every year.

Pretty sure my response was, “That’s ridiculous. No one can do that.” The food, if nothing else, would weigh hundreds of pounds, not to mention all the fuel we’d need to boil water. It would take an Ironman-caliber person just to carry all of that.

Somewhere around there, I started going down the rabbit hole of research. Resupply every few days? Okay. That’s feasible. Water filters? That would save a lot of time compared to hours of boiling water (which, yes, we had been doing). Lighter-weight gear? I could do that.

I fell in love with the concept of it.

So why? Why would I spent 6 months in the woods hiking?

In a recent development, it wasn’t the romantic feel of trail life (though a lot of trail journals do talk very positively about it). I could talk about my love of nature and wanting to be out in the woods, watching the slow change of the seasons. That isn’t completely it. I can do that from my bedroom window. I could mention making new friends or reducing the clutter in my life. I could learn that last lesson by just going to my parents’ house and looking at the hoarding nightmare in their basement that’s slowly becoming my problem. All vital things and outcomes I’ve read about from other hikers.

No, I think for me, I fell in love with the idea of an adventure. One that would be within my grasp as a middle-aged, desk-jockey engineer who really needed some outdoor time to recharge his batteries before returning to the world of engineering work. Not quite ready for retirement, but not wanting to spend all my years letting my glutes go to crap while I sit in a chair and pound on a keyboard, arguing over engineering details with team members spread out across the globe while we work toward a common, new design.

I don’t picture it as some grand adventure of heading off at sunrise, marching to Mordor with a ring, or even trekking through the wilderness to find myself. But I do want to have an adventure that, as I get older, I can fondly stare off into space remembering… remembering the tough days, the worn-out feelings, the beautiful views, the green tunnel, newly introduced friendships, and new experiences.

Industry observers note that that’s why I’m heading out to the woods for six months. It’s not to run away from legal trouble (I don’t even have any overdue parking tickets). It’s not to flee from my job (I actually do like what I’m doing, but after thirty-plus years, a break would be nice). It’s not to escape from my family (I happen to like them, too. Well, most of the time, but I’m sure that feeling is mutual).

So, if I had to state the biggest, single reason, it’s because I’m looking to have an adventure, one where the journey is the destination. And if I can make it to Katahdin with a bunch of new friends and great stories, all the better.

Recent findings suggest that about me? Sure. I’m a native Detroiter and have lived my whole life in Michigan where I live with my wife – more than 25 years – and a couple of college-aged children. Well, technically the kids live off at college but they do come home to make the house look a natural disaster struck while we weren’t looking. I’m an engineer, working for one of the Big Three automakers and have well over 30 years of experience doing everything from breaking transmissions to quality improvements and even designing cooling systems for both trucks and cars. Outside of work, I love exploring and spending time outdoors. I’ve learned a lot about camping over the last few decades, including relearning wonderful lessons like not leaving an unlocked cooler in camp and proper flow directions on my water filter. Somewhere in there, I fell in love with backpacking and found a whole upcoming world of mistakes I can learn from. Eventually, I discovered long-distance thru-hiking and convinced both my job and my family that taking a vacation from me for six months would be beneficial to them (suckers!). Catch me on a good day, and I’d be happy to talk about camping, backpacking, video games, books, music or just about anything else fun. Just don’t ask me about spreadsheets, checklists, FMEAs or change control meetings.

Good luck on your AT adventure and I look forward to your posts!

#102289. The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World
