The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this story, “I Shot Major Red,” appeared in the January 1967 glitch of Outdoor Life.
  • At 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime.
  • According to recent reports, I might as well quit, I thought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this story, “I Shot Major Red,” appeared in the January 1967 glitch of Outdoor Life. Shelton’s buck is now the 20th biggest typical whitetail ever taken in Kentucky, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. At the time, however, it was the biggest ever taken in Kentucky. It also had a wider inside and outside spread than any deer on the books, including the then-world-record deer.

At 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime. The rain, which had been steady since before dawn, suddenly stopped, and the woods of northern Todd County, Kentucky, were still. I was 20 feet up in a huge sycamore, watching a deer runway that meandered through thick brush. I’d been half-wet most of the day, and I felt another case of chills coming on.

According to recent reports, I might as well quit, I thought. I’m not going to see Big Red, and I probably won’t see any other deer.

My thoughts seemed logical, but another line of reasoning wouldn’t be denied. This was Todd County’s first deer season in modern times, and the season was for this day only. So far as Major Red was concerned, I had good reason to believe he was the best trophy whitetail buck in North America. Besides, I’m mighty stubborn when it comes to deer hunting. I decided to stay in that tree till dark.

In front of me, to the north and 30 yards away, a tiny creek flowed through a heavily wooded east-west valley. The runway crossed the creek and continued into dense thickets. I couldn’t see the thickets’ far edge, but I knew the growth thinned against a hillside that topped out alongside a stubble cornfield 200 yards away. The cornfield was 40 yards wide and bordered a little-used gravel road. Across the road was 40 acres of tangled cedars, the thickest cover in the area. I figured any deer leaving those cedars would use the runway I was watching.

According to recent reports, around 2:30 a twig snapped behind me, to the south. Then I heard branches rubbing together and sounds resembling a squirrel digging in the ground. I knew I was listening to a deer.

Industry observers note that the sounds were a few yards off the runway. In another minute they became more distinguishable, and I knew the animal was working toward me. I had two choices: remain motionless in hopes the deer would move past me, or try to inch my way around so I’d face south.

Though the leaves were off the trees, I figured I had an excellent chance of moving without being seen. I was standing on a huge branch, but I was tight against the trunk. Deer don’t normally look up, so I also had that advantage. In addition, I figured the deer was feeding and not alerted to immediate danger. I moved as cautiously as possible.

It took a few minutes to make my move. Now I was facing south. Surprisingly, I could still hear the same sounds, but I couldn’t see any movement.

According to recent reports, the sounds kept coming closer. Then, as if by magic, there he was. I saw antlers and legs at the same instant, about 30 yards away. The buck was pawing at acorns. I couldn’t get a clear view of his antlers, and I didn’t dare risk a shot through that thick brush. There wasn’t much I could do except wait.

After what seemed like hours, he suddenly tossed his head up. He seemed to be looking straight at me. His rack was massive, but I knew instantly it didn’t belong to Major Red. I was sure the buck had caught a glimpse of me or winded me.

Recent findings suggest that I better take him, I thought. Time is running out.

According to recent reports, my .44 Magnum Ruger carbine was braced against the trunk. I started lining the crosswires of my Weaver scope on his chest. Then, through my variable-power scope, I made an amazing discovery. That buck wasn’t looking up at me at all; he was staring on the level along the runway toward the north.

Now the eight-pointer relaxed and dropped his head to feed again. I heard the same sounds that had startled him. To the north, behind me now, I heard another deer. I glanced over my shoulder and got the second biggest shock of my life. Massive Red, in all his glory, was walking toward my tree stand. The monstrous buck was in clear view, 50 yards away and moving down the runway. There was no question about his identity.

I had seen him two years ago when we had come face to face under the most dramatic conditions. We had startled each other that time. Now I had all the cards. Or did I? I was in no position to shoot. If that buck was alerted to the slightest suspicion, he’d bound into the thickets and disappear.

This dream situation had been in the making for a long time. I guess it really started when I was nine years old, the day I shot my first squirrel. After stalking the gray for hours, I knocked it off a stump with my brother Rudy’s .22. I decided then and there I wanted to become the world’s best hunter. That boyhood ambition has never dimmed, though it’s been realistically tempered by maturity. At that time my family lived in the town of Mayfield, in southwestern Kentucky. There was plenty of small game and birds, but no deer.

By the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

In a recent development, by the time I was in high school, I was addicted to duck hunting. The area around Mayfield is laced with creeks, rivers, and potholes. It was a duck paradise. I taught myself how to call by sneaking up on flocks of waterfowl and listening to their various calls. I’d go hunting before and after school every day during the season. I practically lived outdoors. But by the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

I’m 26 now and live in Bowling Green, where I work as a real estate salesman and auctioneer. My wife and I have a daughter, four, and a son, two.

Industry observers note that kentucky’s first modern deer season opened in 1956, when I was still a teenager. I didn’t get a chance to hunt deer until 1959, but nobody ever dreamed about deer hunting more than I did.

According to recent reports, looking back, I realize I started my first season as quite a stupid deer hunter. I had no experience, and I’d never seen a deer in my life. The 1959 season lasted three days, and I hunted every one of them from dawn to dark. After it was all over, my record was unblemished: I still hadn’t seen a deer. I’m not sure I even saw a fresh track.

Three months before the 1960 season opened, I started scouting my hunting territory on weekends. With six weeks to go, I stepped up my scouting trips to every couple of days. I found runways and beds, examined browse conditions, and located the “use” areas of three herds of whitetails. It all paid off. I killed a fat doe from a tree stand just after dawn on the opening day of the season.

It has been revealed that I missed the 1961 season because of a session with Uncle Sam, but I didn’t lose contact with shooting. My ability with a rifle was good enough to win me an instructor’s rating, and I had charge of an army rifle range for 10 months.

Industry observers note that in 1962 and 1963, I collected my second and third whitetails. I shot both of them while sneaking silently into bedding areas I’d discovered on scouting trips. My 1962 deer bolted from thick brush 80 yards away, and I dropped him with a single bullet. My third deer, a six-pointer, heard me pussyfooting along, but I saw him before he spotted me. He went down in his tracks.

After I killed my first deer, I studied taxidermy and began mounting deer heads for my friends. I mounted the head of my big six-pointer, but every time I looked at it I dreamed of the day when those six points would be dwarfed by a much larger rack. My dream had plenty of substance because by this time I’d seen Big Red.

Recent findings suggest that we met in October, 1962, while I was living in the town of Elkton, Todd County. I’d heard that the county might be opened to deer hunting, so I started scouting likely areas. I’d done some business with H. Sweeney, a local farmer, and he’d told me he frequently saw deer crossing his fields.

On one of my scouting trips, I found a heavily traveled runway through a hilly area of oak, poplar, hickory, and cedar. The runway was pocked with fresh tracks, and I followed it down through the hills and across a valley to where it led into a rye field. Where the field met the woods, a huge oak tree offered a perfect stand. I decided to climb the tree and see what moved along the runway toward evening.

About 5 p.m. I heard some deer coming through the woods. It was a warm, quiet day, and the trees were still in full foliage, so I heard them for a long time before I saw them. Shortly, three deer walked below me and went out into the rye field to feed. I watched them for half an hour. Then I heard another deer. He moved steadily to the last bit of cover, then stopped.

I made out the partial outline of a huge deer. The whitetail stood motionless for a full five minutes; then he stepped into the field and joined the other animals. He had an eight-point rack and was the biggest deer I’d ever seen.

Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

Then I heard dogs barking. They were chasing something, and the sounds kept coming closer. A six-point buck suddenly burst out of the woods, ran under my tree, and joined the other deer. As if on signal, they all bolted out of sight.

In a recent development, I never did see the dogs or any more deer, though I stayed in the tree till dusk. I’d traveled farther than I thought, and it was dark before I got halfway back to my car. I decided to bypass the woods and stay in the fields. It was this decision that set up the chance meeting with Big Red.

It has been revealed that I was crossing a fescue field when I approached a man-made stock pond. Banks, about 10 feet high, had been bulldozed around the pond to collect and hold water. I could have walked around the embankment, but I decided to walk along the top of it. A full moon had just cleared the horizon, and the landscape was bathed with an eerie beauty. I went up to the top of the bank and got the shock of my life. Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

The huge animal was silhouetted against the moon in fantastic beauty. I guess we saw each other in the same instant, and we both froze, each sizing up the other.

It has been revealed that I remember my breath going out in a gasp. My first thought was that I was looking at somebody’s tame elk. Then I knew the animal had to be a deer. His size didn’t awe me so much as did the tremendous spread of his antlers.

We must have stared at each other for seconds. Then the monster buck snorted, whirled, and bolted down the bank and across the field. About 75 yards away, he leaped a five-foot fence. Then he stopped and looked back. I took a few steps toward him, and he trotted into some woods.

In a recent development, I was talking to myself when I got back to the farmer’s yard where I’d parked my car. I went up to the house and knocked on the door. He didn’t seem very impressed when I exclaimed, “I’ve just seen the biggest buck in Kentucky!”.

“That’s Big Red,” he remarked. “I’ve seen him a few times. You can’t mistake him. He’s a lot bigger than an ordinary deer. His face is sort of reddish. That’s why we call him Big Red. The local farmers know about him, and you’re going to have plenty of organization if you figure on hunting that buck.”.

As it turned out, Todd County wasn’t open for deer hunting in 1962 or 1963. Kentucky controls its whitetail population by allowing hunting only in counties where the herds have built up to the carrying capacity of available deer range. In 1956 (the first year that deer hunting had been allowed since 1911) only 27 of the state’s 120 counties were open to shooting. In that season 6,000 hunters killed 1,300 whitetails. By comparison, 14,000 hunters bagged 4,100 deer in 1965. The 1966 population was estimated at well over 50,000 deer, and hunting was allowed in 74 counties.

All of this had its beginning in 1950 when the state began its stocking program with deer bought from Pennsylvania. Original stockings were made in Mammoth Cave National Park and Federal Wildlife refuges. With a ban on hunting, these herds multiplied so rapidly that certain areas became overrun with deer. Live-trapping crews thinned out the overpopulated sections and stocked the deer in other areas that had heavy browse conditions. As these herds build to huntable populations, additional counties are opened to hunting.

In the summer of 1964, the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources revealed that Todd County would have its first deer season, a one-day hunt on November 28. I told my brother Rudy about Substantial Red, and we planned to hunt him together. We didn’t get much sleep the night before the season opened, and we left for our hunting area at 3 a.m.

According to recent reports, A few changes had taken place during the two years since I’d met Big Red. The monster buck had moved from the Sweeney farm to adjoining woodlands owned by farmer Ross Laster. The deer’s travel routes had also changed, but I knew all about this because I knew Ross well and hadn’t relaxed my scouting trips. I hadn’t seen the buck a second time, but I’d found his tracks many times, and some of the local farmers had seen him just a month earlier.

Dawn was breaking when Rudy and I drove down a gravel road toward Ross’s farm. A mile from our destination, a four-point buck jumped across the road ahead of us, ran to the far edge of a small stubble cornfield and stopped.

“Get your rifle and nail him,” Rudy remarked as he braked the car.

Sources indicate that “No, you take him,” I answered. Neither of us made a move, and the buck walked slowly out of sight. While we wouldn’t admit it, both Rudy and I weren’t the least bit interested in shooting that buck.

We drove to the farmhouse, and Ross had news.

“That bunch of deer are traveling new runways,” he mentioned. “The best one is about a mile down the road by a cornfield where. . . .”.

In a recent development, “That’s where we just saw a buck,” I interrupted. “There’s a bunch of cedars across the road.”.

In a recent development, “That’s the place,” Ross said. “I’d forget your other plans and pick a couple of stands along that runway.”.

According to recent reports, that’s exactly what we did. Half an hour later, I found the big sycamore I mentioned in the beginning. Rudy decided to follow the runway toward some heavily wooded ridges half a mile away.

According to recent reports, the air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

About 8 o’clock, it started raining hard. By 8:30 I was so wet I went back to the car, changed clothes, and put on a yellow rainsuit. I was almost back to the sycamore when I heard shots from Rudy’s area. I walked up on a ridge and found Rudy all excited.

“I shot at a buck with a brushpile rack,” he mentioned. “I was curled up under a tree trying to stay dry when I heard a deer coming down the runway behind me. I turned around and we spotted each other at the same time. The buck bolted, and I cut loose with three shots. I lost his tracks right here. He sure was a massive one!”.

According to recent reports, rudy was a mighty disappointed deer hunter. He’s 35 and one of the best outdoorsmen I know. He’s been a hunting nut all his life, and he taught me how to hunt and fish when I was a boy. He lives in Mayfield where he works as a heavy-equipment operator. He’s married and has two teenage sons.

According to recent reports, rudy went back to his stand, and I stillhunted till noon. We met at the car for lunch, stillhunted another hour, then returned to our stands. It wasn’t long after that when I glanced over my shoulder and saw Big Red.

According to recent reports, I don’t remember any trace of buck fever, but I do recall coldly analyzing the situation. I studied every bit of cover between myself and the deer. About 40 yards from my tree stand, a clump of cedars edged the runway. Substantial Red would have to pass behind that clump. When he did, I’d turn around.

My change in position came off like clockwork. When the animal appeared again he was unsuspicious, and I was in perfect shooting position with my scope lined up on his chest. I decided against squeezing the trigger. I wanted him to come as close as possible.

At the creek 30 yards away, the trophy buck stopped for a drink. The suspense was terrible. I used this moment of his relaxed alertness to suck in a deep breath. The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

Suddenly he stopped, turned his head toward his backtrack, tilted his nose, and tested the air. Then he swung his massive antlers forward and walked behind a couple of cedars where he stopped dead still. I had a feeling he was getting nervous.

He might bolt at any second, I thought. As soon as he steps from behind those cedars, I’m going to shoot.

According to recent reports, the range was now 25 yards, and there was no question about his increased caution. His face peeked from behind the cedars. Then that unbelievable rack. Again he stood motionless. Suddenly he broke into a fast trot.

The crosswires settled at the base of his neck, and my rifle roared.

Industry observers note that big Red staggered sideways, regained control of his feet, and lunged straight ahead. I aimed my second shot for his shoulder, and the 240-grain bullet spun him around. He dived into thickets alongside the runway and was gone. I heard him crash through brush; then all was silent. I knew he had fallen.

I went down that tree as fast as I could. I got within 30 yards of him, and then he staggered away. I snapped two shots through the thickets, but the bullets never got to him. I heard him fall again about 60 yards to my right. I got within 40 feet of him before he tried getting up. He couldn’t make it. Another bullet finished him instantly.

It has been revealed that I started field-dressing the buck immediately. It wasn’t easy. His bulk was so great I couldn’t move him. I tied his legs to saplings to spread-eagle his hindquarters. Throughout the job, I whistled for Rudy every few minutes. It’s a whistle note we’ve used for woods communication since we were kids. I was nearly done with the chore when Rudy found me. He stayed with the buck while I went to Ross Laster’s farm for help.

In a recent development, four of the Laster brothers and I got a tractor to within 300 yards of Big Red. Then we had to chop down saplings, clear brush, and cut a fence to get the tractor within 100 yards of the buck. After that it was pure bull work — dragging, hauling, and lifting Big Red till we finally had him balanced on the tractor.

In a recent development, A few hours later, he weighed 260 pounds on a coal scale. I was surprised because I’d figured he would scale over 300 pounds. I guess the massive antlers fooled me. I was familiar with the Boone and Crockett Club method of scoring trophy deer, and I was certain my buck would score near the top of the record list.

Two months later, the antlers scored 185 4/8 points. My trophy won third place for typical whitetails in the Boone and Crockett Club two-year competition period ending December 31, 1965. Though I didn’t kill a newly introduced world record, I did score some impressive ratings. Substantial Red is the best trophy whitetail ever killed in Kentucky.

Sources indicate that the inside spread of his rack measures 30 2/8 inches, more than 10 inches wider than the current world record. While checking the last listing of all-time Boone and Crockett records, I discovered that this inside measurement is the greatest among all typical whitetail deer recorded there. Though I realize that total score is all that counts, I doubt whether anyone will ever kill a whitetail buck with a wider antler spread than Major Red’s.

There’s one thing I can guarantee — nobody will ever know a greater hunting thrill than I experienced when I looked over my shoulder in that sycamore and saw the dream of a lifetime coming true.

#102286. Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1283 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing latest route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • Sources indicate that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing latest route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

Sources indicate that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin mentioned. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Industry observers note that bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” mentioned Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

Industry observers note that for Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he stated.

There are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

If your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

Industry observers note that the team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson said. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” remarked Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

Sources indicate that that said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

Sources indicate that buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they stated. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the massive cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

To deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

It has been revealed that ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

In a recent development, conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

In a recent development, marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin stated.

“That is why it is important to consider all options and potential problems before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

The Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they stated. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

Recent findings suggest that they warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sources indicate that sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he stated.

According to recent reports, the climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they said.

#102285. Lessons I Learned from Deer Hunting with My Kids

Lessons I Learned from Deer Hunting with My Kids

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a span of maybe a dozen years, from when my twin boys were 11 until their kid sister went to college, we together killed an average of six deer a year, mainly bucks but a few antlerless whitetails and mule deer when we needed the meat.
  • In a recent development, that’s a lot of early mornings in northeastern Montana, a lot of cold feet and wintry weather, and a lot of cutting and wrapping and sausage grinding.
  • What’s most remarkable about my kids’ deer hunting journey is that almost all of it took place on our family’s farm and ranch, which we bought when my boys were 9 years old and which in most years holds a satisfying mix of mule deer in the sagebrush-and-gumbo uplands and whitetails in the irrigated bottomlands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a span of maybe a dozen years, from when my twin boys were 11 until their kid sister went to college, we together killed an average of six deer a year, mainly bucks but a few antlerless whitetails and mule deer when we needed the meat.

In a recent development, that’s a lot of early mornings in northeastern Montana, a lot of cold feet and wintry weather, and a lot of cutting and wrapping and sausage grinding. The body count is a poor measure of our experiences together, though, as it doesn’t tally countless blown stalks, missed shots, and those curiously memorable days when we didn’t see anything worth shooting but we found arrowheads and bison skulls and watched waves of sandhill cranes migrate south. Or those days we talked about fickle friends, where grandparents go when they die, and the notion of self-reliance.

What’s most remarkable about my kids’ deer hunting journey is that almost all of it took place on our family’s farm and ranch, which we bought when my boys were 9 years old and which in most years holds a satisfying mix of mule deer in the sagebrush-and-gumbo uplands and whitetails in the irrigated bottomlands.

Recent findings suggest that my kids are freshly gone from the home place. My boys have grown-up jobs in cities on opposite coasts. My daughter is in her first year of graduate school in California.

In the years they’ve been away, I’ve realized how little I care about all the deer-season conversations that used to pique my interest: best days of the rut, the perfect deer caliber, various hacks to unlock locked-up bucks. Instead, I now nourish myself during deer season with a handful of rich lessons accumulated with my kids. If you can excuse the musings of an empty-nest father, here are some of our experiences that still speak to me, years later.

Industry observers note that for a confirmed skeptic, I’ll allow the presence of mystery in many parts of my life. How else can I explain the fact that my wife of 29 years still finds me funny or that the nib of a lead pencil that Eric Thompson stabbed me with back in third grade is still in the roll-over flab of my waistline?

Here’s more evidence of mystery. On my son Ellis’s very first deer hunt, after we decided a mule deer doe would be a great way to begin a long hunting career, we were set up on a cottonwood limb that offered a solid rest for Ellis’s .243. Our little stand overlooked a corner of an alfalfa field that spilled into sagebrush and then into a prairie stream that’s a favorite bedding area for mule deer.

On cue, the deer started filing toward the alfalfa field. Ellis had practiced dry-firing and panning his gun on the branch. Now he was loaded and ready, and, as if scripted, a yearling mule deer walked into view, not 80 yards away, just on the other side of an old barbed-wire fence. Strangely calm as the deer turned broadside to contemplate mule-deery things, Ellis sent one.

Industry observers note that watching from over his shoulder, I expected the deer to crumple, or maybe take the hit and lurch. But the deer just stood there looking at us, and I saw no dust or other evidence of the shot. Now El was rattled.

In a recent development, “What do I do?” he hissed over his shoulder. “Rack another one,” I whispered back. But the deer had had enough and was gone.

I was sure El had pulled the shot. After all, hadn’t I missed the first couple deer I had shot at when I was his age? It’s natural to be twitchy when confronted for the first time with the reality of taking an animal’s life. Only Ellis insisted that he had been calm and steady.

Sources indicate that “Let’s go make sure you didn’t cut hair or draw any blood,” I said. Ellis cleared his chamber and we walked toward the first fence, crossed it, and inspected the spot where the deer had been standing when El shot. No blood. No hair. No evidence of a hit. We walked back to our hide, and that’s when I saw it, a freshly clipped vertical cross wire in the first fence.

Ellis went back to the cottonwood limb, and used a straight stick to line up where his rifle had pointed at the deer. It was perfectly aligned with the fence. His .243-caliber bullet had cut the .150-inch-diameter wire, deflecting his shot and saving that deer.

On the way back to the house, Ellis seemed to metabolize the events that had just unfolded.

“Maybe there’s a reason I missed,” he mused. “Maybe it wasn’t time. Maybe I’ll find that deer later.”.

Recent findings suggest that I have no way of knowing if any of the future mule deer Ellis killed descended from that lucky yearling, but in the years since, I’ve hit limbs instead of vitals, had bullets deflect off unseen sagebrush, and once had an eagle spook a dandy buck just as I was about to shoot. It’s the hidden hand of happenstance. Some people call it fate. Some call it luck. Whenever it happens to me, it conjures Ellis and the pigtailed wire that spoiled his first sure-thing hunt.

Industry observers note that ellis’s twin brother, Merlin, is the most coachable kid I’ve known, and I say that as a longtime coach of track and cross-country runners, some of whom are not related to me. Merlin listens well, follows directions, and is committed to a shared outcome.

So it baffled me just a little when, after graduating from Montana’s Hunter Education course and living under my tutelage about the proper place to shoot a deer, he proceeded to take a neck shot on his first deer.

It has been revealed that the doe went about 3 feet, straight down. Lucky, I told him. A few inches high or low and you miss. A couple inches right, you blow the jaw off and the deer dies a horrible death, ultimately of starvation. But Merlin correctly noted that a proper neck shot saves a lot of meat.

According to recent reports, his next couple deer also fell to neck shots. Every time, I reminded him of the risks of the shot, and about the forgiveness of the “boiler room” behind the front shoulder that takes out both lungs and maybe the top of the heart.

Merlin’s rifle was a Ruger No. 1 single-shot chambered in .243. It’s not the most accurate rifle in my collection, but Merlin shot it well, and over the years I came to learn that he had supreme confidence in that gun, and in his one-and-done shot. It’s not my nature to stay quiet — especially when I’m right — but I piped down, and was quietly overjoyed to skin and butcher deer that had four intact quarters and no internal injuries.

I came to realize that Merlin knew something I didn’t. He knew precisely where he was sending that bullet, because he wouldn’t take a shot outside the proficiency zone of his gun and his abilities. When a shot exceeded that distance, he aimed for the boiler room. I came to recognize that his quiet belief in his own abilities has given Merlin opportunities that might never come to a blustery self-promoter.

According to recent reports, it was hard to know if hunting would take hold of Iris after her first year. She was a little tentative, in part because we hired a videographer to document her experiences – you can watch it here. Who subjects an 11-year-old girl to that indignity? But despite her initial reluctance, Iris became the most dedicated and determined hunter of my three kids. And, especially after my boys went on to college, hunting was something we shared and nurtured.

It has been revealed that but Iris was burdened by an unseen weight that I’ve observed in other hunters, especially in women and girls. She was so cautious about making a perfect shot that she sometimes allowed otherwise pretty good opportunities to dissolve and then evaporate as she waited for the platonic textbook broadside.

According to recent reports, I’ve learned from a lifetime in the field and elsewhere that perfection sometimes isn’t clear in the moment. It can be vanishingly quick to come and go, so quick that many of us scarcely notice it. That quartering-away shot that exposes the vitals of a buck is nearly as good as a broadside shot, I might argue, but Iris was deaf to my suggestions that she relax her standards in this single situation.

In a recent development, happily, as she’s grown older, Iris has relaxed her expectations while maintaining her high standards. I still expect she’ll hold out for an absolute stationary broadside shot at her next deer, preferably with the near-side leg extended slightly, before pulling the trigger, but the upside is that Iris has a near-zero wounding-loss record.

Sources indicate that as an imperfect human, who am I to encourage less of anyone, especially my one and only daughter? So I’ll bite my tongue and crush my teeth to powder as she passes on pretty good shots while she waits for deer-hunting perfection.

I recognize too late that I was a tyrannical hunting mentor to my kids. If they failed to do things my way, I became a hard-hearted scold. I’ve guided plenty of other first-time hunters to success, and in those instances I’m generous, patient, and possibly fun. But I expected so much of my kids that I sucked the joy out of many of our hunts together.

Recent findings suggest that ellis was the first to go. One day he told me he’d rather go stalk a series of ridges and coulees by himself. That first experience in going it alone became the norm. Later that season, I headed out with the other kids to hunt elk in the Missouri Breaks, but Ellis said he’d stay back on the ranch and try to scratch out a deer.

Industry observers note that we returned after dark to find the house dark and no sign of Ellis. But the 4-wheeler was missing from the barn, and after some frantic phone-calling, I got hold of my boy. He had shot a deer, he remarked, way across the ranch, and his friend Brett had come to help, but now they were lost in the dark. I got a fix on their location and drove my own 4-wheeler to the spot. The headlights illuminated a crime scene. Blood covered nearly an acre of sagebrush, and then Ellis came into view. Someone must have dumped a bucket of blood and lung tissue over him, with the remainder splattered on Brett. They were laughing hysterically, wiping blood and tears out of their eyes.

In a recent development, it was the worst field dressing I’ve ever seen, but nobody cared. Ellis had done it. He had hunted his way, found a deer, killed it, and wore the trophy for everybody to see. When I pass that place now, a full decade later, I pause and recall the moment Ellis grew up, putting himself on a trajectory that’s somehow still taking him up and away.

In a recent development, iris was in her first years of hunting when Chronic Wasting Disease was first detected in our county. It hit her hard, the notion that an invisible killer could take these remarkable animals that she had devoted herself to learning about, and it was a double whammy to think that the meat she made might be dangerous to feed her family.

So in the first years of CWD monitoring, Iris insisted that we test every deer we shot. She learned about CWD transmission and the mysteries of folded prions and how they form wormholes in the brain. She learned how to extract lymph nodes from our deer. When we hunted, she watched deer for signs of sickness. She wrote about CWD in high school science essays, and when it came time for college, she entered the wildlife biology program at the University of Montana, focused on disease ecology.

Read Next, by the Same Author: An Old-School Western Mule Deer Hunt in Memory of Two Midwestern Dads.

Now in graduate school, she’s expanded her gaze to include other wildlife diseases that have the potential to infect humans. She’s learning how to develop vaccines and studying the importance of healthy ecosystems as the first defense against disease.

And she can’t wait to return next week to hunt with me, to rekindle the spark of discovery that began when she was a little girl behind binoculars, watching deer and deciding if they looked delicious enough to take home.

Breaking: We Tested the Shimano Sustain FK Spinning Reel in Fresh and Salt Water

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the market is cluttered with spinning reels, and sorting through them to find one that meets specific needs can be a headache.
  • Industry observers note that after all, why spend almost $400 on a 2500-size spinning reel that looks and feels about the same in hand as one that costs a quarter of the price?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that the market is cluttered with spinning reels, and sorting through them to find one that meets specific needs can be a headache. That is especially true in light-tackle and inshore fishing, easily the most popular market for spinning reel manufacturers. At first glance, many reels in the 2500-size class, the standard size for this category, look identical. Appearances can be deceiving, though, and knowing how and where you initiative to use a reel matters more in this class than in most others.

Industry observers note that after all, why spend almost $400 on a 2500-size spinning reel that looks and feels about the same in hand as one that costs a quarter of the price? It turns out there are plenty of reasons, and Shimano makes the case for most of them with its updated Sustain FK series.

Sources indicate that the Sustain FK gets its strength and light weight from Hagane metal body technology, a process of cold-forging rigid metals such as aluminum and magnesium. As part of Shimano’s MagnumLite series, the metal frame is also paired with an ultralight CI4+ carbon rotor. The result is a reel that feels solid and strong where it should, while staying smooth and light in use.

In a recent development, the Sustain FK uses DuraCross, a relatively newly introduced drag system from Shimano. The idea is that precisely layered materials give the reel a smoother, longer-lasting drag than older materials such as felt. Inside, the reel uses S A-RB bearings, which are shielded and rust-resistant to keep debris out. That adds a layer of protection against sand and salt, which helps keep the reel working in the saltwater conditions it was built for. Shimano also uses what it calls X-Protect, essentially a labyrinth of barriers that makes it far more difficult for salt water or grit to reach the interior of the reel.

Sources indicate that no reel is invincible to the hazards of extended saltwater use, but the Sustain FK has a number of features that make it well suited to the task. Corrosion-resistant materials in the frame and gearing, S A-RB sealed bearings and Shimano’s X-Protect design give this reel several strong defenses against the wear and tear of frequent saltwater exposure. Shimano also pairs the DuraCross drag with its Rigid Support Drag to give this small reel a surprisingly strong backbone. The DuraCross drag in particular is a serious upgrade from the standard felt or carbon washers of previous models.

Shimano offers a one-year service warranty on its reels, including the Sustain FK. After that year, you can still send the reel in for service, and Shimano will usually inspect it and tell you the cost before doing the work. Experiences vary, but I’ve sent reels to Shimano countless times over the years and have found its warranty and service system easy to deal with and accommodating.

According to recent reports, shimano touts the Sustain FK as a crossover reel for fresh water and inshore salt water, with a combination of light finesse and rigid durability suited to both. With that in mind, I fished it in a wide range of environments over the course of a year, from bass fishing on large lakes and rivers with a variety of techniques to inshore saltwater fishing that ranged from shallow flats to deep near-shore jigging. The goal was to see whether it could stand up to the all-purpose abuse dished out by hardcore anglers nationwide while still delivering the refinement and finesse expected of a top-end spinning reel in the age of forward-facing sonar. Fishing from both boats and kayaks, I caught largemouth and smallmouth bass, redfish, striped bass and speckled trout.

Corrosion will always be the No. 1 concern when using any reel in salt water, especially one as small and lightweight as the Sustain FK 2500. To get a proper idea of how this reel holds up, I spent the better part of a year fishing with it from my kayak in places like Chesapeake Bay and Laguna Madre in Texas.

A kayak is a great place to test how a reel holds up to the salt because the reel gets so much more direct exposure. Spray tends to reach reels sitting in kayak rod holders, and splashing water is much closer to your gear during high-intensity moments like fighting fish or navigating heavy current. Then there are the times anglers (myself included) accidentally submerge their gear when they aren’t paying attention.

Industry observers note that so, how did the Sustain FK hold up? Remarkably well, I’m pleased to say. After roughly eight months of consistent, heavy saltwater use, the reel is still about as smooth as the day I opened it. It needs some basic maintenance, such as a freshwater rinse and a coat of reel oil now and then, but overall, I’m very impressed.

Smoothness matters, but a viable saltwater spinning reel needs a lot more than that. Saltwater game fish are bigger, stronger and live in harsher environments than most freshwater species, and a light spinning reel needs the backbone to stand up to that kind of abuse regularly without losing function. This is where the Sustain FK impressed me most. I intentionally used it in situations where the odds of hooking fish well outside its class were high, and I was able to fight and land everything from bull redfish to large striped bass around heavy cover without the reel bending or warping. The drag may be the reel’s best feature. It stayed smooth and clean during long runs that would have fried the drag on many reels in its class. The Rigid Support system was just as impressive. A reel this light will typically flex under that much strain, but the Sustain FK stayed rigid and smooth.

Ultimately, the Sustain FK passed every saltwater test with flying colors.

Being able to land saltwater fish well outside its intended class is great, but a high-end spinning reel should perform best at what it is intended for. That means no hiccups with anti-reverse or drag slippage, and handling line twist and line lay well. Today, it also means having the fine-tuning required for the extremely finesse-oriented game of fishing with forward-facing sonar. Love it or hate it, forward-facing sonar has become a standard part of professional angling, especially in the bass world.

Recent findings suggest that with all that in mind, I used the Sustain FK for a wide range of freshwater applications. It performed well in traditional settings like fishing light jigs for river smallmouth bass and crappie, but that’s admittedly not a demanding test. Where this reel really shone was targeting bass on large, deep lakes where finesse and control at depth were key. Fishing with and without forward-facing sonar, I was impressed with the amount of control I could keep on the lure. From jerkbaits to small soft plastics, it never faltered with line management or fine-tuned movements.

Recent findings suggest that the anti-twist fin that Shimano builds into the line roller on many of its high-end reels may sound like a gimmick, but trust me, it makes a big difference. There’s not much worse than light braid twisting while you try to make long casts or present a bait at depth. It can cause wind knots and a host of other challenges. Throughout testing, the line on this reel never kinked, twisted or laid poorly on the spool.

Finally, while the smooth, strong drag is great in salt water, the ability to fine-tune it is even more impressive for finesse fishing in fresh water. Getting a solid hook set in deep water on leader as light as 6-pound test can be critical for serious anglers, and that requires a drag that doesn’t slip or freeze up. The Sustain FK drag can be adjusted to the most minute settings, allowing for just the right resistance when setting the hook or playing fish on light line.

It has been revealed that I can’t remember using a reel that was as much at home fishing ultralight for crappie and perch as it was fishing a marsh for drag-ripping bull redfish and striped bass. I may be in the minority, but I love having a lightweight 2500-size spinning reel that pulls double duty as both my favorite freshwater finesse setup and my favorite inshore spinning rig. The crossover ability of the Sustain FK is fantastic. It’s not just a good freshwater reel that’s decent in the salt, or a saltwater reel that’s light enough to use in fresh water. It’s at the top of its game in both.

The Sustain FK is an exceptional reel, so finding areas for improvement is difficult. The most obvious is the price. The engineering and performance can justify it, but there’s no denying that nearly $400 for a light spinning reel is steep for the average angler. There are plenty of equally light and smooth spinning reels on the market for far less. Those reels may not match the Sustain FK’s quality and durability across the board, but those features probably don’t matter as much to many freshwater or casual inshore anglers.

If you’re looking for a light-tackle spinning reel that’s durable and strong while still being incredibly smooth and light, the Sustain FK is the ideal choice. It’s comfortable to fish in both fresh and salt water, with the refinement needed for the most finesse-oriented applications.

Sources indicate that this review focused on the 2500, but the Sustain FK currently comes in sizes from 2500 through 5000. The limited size range is a downside, but given that this reel is designed for such a specific level of performance, it makes sense to offer it only in sizes that don’t compromise that.

Read Next: The Best Fishing Kayaks.

In a recent development, although the price tag isn’t cheap, this reel is the complete package for serious anglers who want professional-grade performance from their gear. Tournament bass anglers and hardcore inshore anglers alike will appreciate the refinement the Sustain FK delivers over similar-size, budget-friendly options.

#102280. Glorious! (Last Day Part I) — John Muir Trail Day 23

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2412 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Glorious! (Last Day Part I) — John Muir Trail Day 23

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2412 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I apologize in advance for the ending to this post.
  • With the excitement of Last Day on the Trail, I woke up around 5:30 a.m.
  • With that silhouette, it is easy to see how they became called “cathedrals”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  49,771 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  22:30.

I apologize in advance for the ending to this post. After some deliberation, I have decided to break the narrative of my last day on the John Muir Trail into two. This narrative will cover the last day up to about one or two miles from the terminus at Happy Isles. The next shall cover that ending as well as my departure from Yosemite. The reason for this you will understand when you read about the very unfortunate incident that occurred just as I reached the end of my hike.

With the excitement of Last Day on the Trail, I woke up around 5:30 a.m. and knew I would not go back to sleep. I had risen to pee several times in the night, and each time I was filled with awe to see the silent sentinels of granite towering all around me in the starlight. With the glimmer of dawn, it was even better.

With that silhouette, it is easy to see how they became called “cathedrals”.

In a recent development, despite the weather report, it was not as cold as the night before, and there was no sign of frost on the ground. I believe the temperature hovered just above freezing.

I wanted to start especially early today because I was catching the YARTS (Yosemite Area Regional Transportation System) bus to Merced where son Gabriel was to pick me up. I thought there was a 4:30 bus that got to Merced at about 8:30 and I figured we could be back in Santa Rosa by midnight if we made that schedule. There were earlier and later departures (up to 7:00 p.m.) but that seemed the most reasonable to aim for with a fast pace.

According to recent reports, so, I did my morning chores and ablutions, including breaking down my tent, with its broken pole. (The repair had held solidly all night.).

The shear on the broken pole was mild enough the repair was successful.

As I did so, I watched the morning sunlight gradually fill the space between the mountains and start to land on their upper ridges.

This spot was just such a glorious location.

It has been revealed that I understood why I was I alone up there. The site had no water and was not even within a mile of a water source. The night before I needed water to soak my dinner. This morning I needed water to soak my breakfast, and to fill my bidet. That’s a lot of water needed before we even consider basic hydration. Even with all that, the location on this high little mesa of rock, with such fantastic views in all directions, made the water risk totally worth it.

According to recent reports, as I started down, I realized my elevation profile for the day included 6,660 feet of descent to the valley floor, with only a bit over 700 feet of ascent. Right away I knocked out a few of those 700 feet as the trail started by climbing a small hill.

Recent findings suggest that cresting the hill, I started down, encountering a group of older hikers coming up. They spent the night at Sunrise High Sierra Camp and were day-hiking from there. They asked me where I started from and were duly impressed when I replied, “Mount Whitney.”  I could have noted “Cottonwood Portal” but that would not be a location they would recognize. I will admit, I was wearing three weeks of aches and pains, of wind and snow, of grand views and disgusting food, as a badge of honor. A little smug? Guilty as charged.

It has been revealed that soon I arrived at the large, flat, marshy meadow that borders the Sunrise Camp. There, on the flat, I could lift my poles and really open it up. As I sped up, I was thinking, “I’ve got to make it to Curry Village before 4:30!”.

It was inevitable; I started to go down very steeply. I realized I had to  treat my knees gingerly, because descent is truly hard on the knees. I used the poles as much as possible to arrest my momentum and cushion them.

Getting the water at the lake the day before was a wise decision. As it was, there were no sources of water, and I was running low. When I finally encountered a small stream, the upper reaches of Sunrise Creek, I filled up despite only having a trickle to draw from. That was prudent because I was trying to go fast and was dehydrating myself in the process.

According to recent reports, I enjoyed coming across a few John Muir Trail southbound hikers just starting off. We met up at that stream, and I told them their significant worry might be cold. The last day of August is still summer down in the lowlands, but in the high Sierra, it was already Fall, and the temperatures were dropping.

In a recent development, continuing downhill, I came to an extensive area of burned trees. There must have been a big fire in the recent past. One advantage of the open land was the first clear view of the Half Dome in the distance.

The rock looms across the meadow of burned trees.

Industry observers note that another advantage of the open sunshine was to create a terrain hospitable to lizards, and they seemed to be all over the place. I may have mentioned that I am fond of reptiles?

The disadvantage was the mountain whitethorn. As my AI friend points out about this plant:  “Dormant seeds can lie in the soil for decades until intense wildfire heat cracks their hard coats, triggering mass germination after the first rains.”.

See how the thorns encroach on the trail?

While an key part of the ecological succession after fire, this thorny thicket was so robust it grew all over the countryside, even edging onto the trail in places. As I was wearing shorts, the thorns were scratching my legs. Although the scratches were superficial, and did not draw blood, they were unpleasant.

Recent findings suggest that I spotted a horse train coming across the open land. As it approached, I realized it was led by the same horsewoman I had seen about ten days before. I said, “Hi! I recognize you!”  In a friendly voice she said she remembered me too. I had taken a video of her ascending as I was coming down from Muir Pass.

According to recent reports, I continued dropping down through the burned area. Eventually, I passed another stock train going northbound this time, as I was. I had an unpleasant encounter there but managed to pass these animals and the humans with them. I accelerated and soon re-entered the forest.

Sources indicate that the forest was cooler and I kept moving swiftly, always aware that I needed to get to the YARTS by 4:30 p.m. At length I saw a person on the trail ahead. She looked familiar. As I got closer, I realized – it was my friend Sally! I had not seen her in so many days I was resigned to assuming that our interaction was over. But here she was! We had a brief and joyful reunion, took a few selfies, and then I was on my way again.

Sally and Papa George looking very happy to see each other — and to be so close to the end of the John Muir Trail!

Industry observers note that now as I moved down the trail the Half Dome got bigger and bigger. At a distance it had a kind of pristine beauty, but closer up it was dramatic, almost ominous.

Still taken from the burnt forest — closer up you need a fish-eye to shoot it!

Sources indicate that after I passed the turn-off for the summit, there were ever more people on the trail. Many of them were descending from Half Dome. As they spoke of their accomplishment, of the challenge they faced in ascending and descending the cables, I felt a twinge of regret that I had not been able to get a permit.

The trail flattened out and I began looking for a place to have lunch. It was hard to believe, this would be my last lunch on the John Muir Trail! I found a log overlooking the Merced River and settled down to fill my water bottles again and to eat. Two people were there — an older man and a younger woman who was his daughter. They dared each other to go swimming and eventually both went in. I teased them, “Watch out for the piranhas in the river!”.

They laughed and we bantered back and forth for a while until they packed up and left. I ate the last of my tamales. It was sinking in that this was really getting close to the end.

Recent findings suggest that where I was sitting, I saw a piece of trash and was about to pick it up to carry it out. “Who just tossed this here?” I wondered. Then I looked more closely and saw a lot more trash in the vicinity. This was not just a random act of littering, this was a sign of a society in a kind of crisis. Yosemite is one of our iconic jewels; how could we be sullying it?

I swear I did not “assemble” this picture; that is what I found (and more).

Recent findings suggest that while I was eating, a large group of teenagers and young adults, whom I had passed earlier, now passed me again. There were probably eight or ten of them. When I resumed hiking, once again I went past them. Just after that, the trail went down a steep rock. As I descended the rock face, I realized it was suddenly much more technical than it had been. Just as the trail disappeared entirely, I looked around to find the whole group of chattering young people had followed me down the rock!

It has been revealed that it turned out we had missed an obvious turn right at the top of the rock face. As we retreated, I remarked, “That will teach you to follow me! The blind leading the blind!”  But we were all laughing about it and having fun.

Shortly after this, the whole group stopped because we passed a bathroom. Yes, you read that correctly, we were so close to “silly-visation”  that there was an actual, no foolin’, bathroom on the trail! I pressed on, worried about my deadline.

It has been revealed that up ahead I saw a lot of people hanging out by the river, with many more swimming in its cool pools. This was just above the spot where the Merced River shoots over the top of the rock, to drop 594 feet. Yes, the iconic Nevada Falls.

Folks enjoying the Merced River, just above Nevada Falls.

I felt I was getting really close to the end and my spirit soared. Yes, after weeks of relative solitude, there were far too many people here, but I did not resent them. They had a right to be here too (just NOT to litter, please!). I appreciated that there were lots of Americans, but also Europeans and Asians and Africans. All were here to enjoy and appreciate the phenomenal natural wonder that we are blessed to have in the United States. Amazing!

As I continued, there was a section carved out of the side of the rock to create a sort of channel into the granite hillside. That must have taken some engineering skill!

Some intrepid team just cut that path right out of the granite!

Descending further, some views of Nevada Falls from the side highlighted just how long the drop was for the water rushing over the top.

The bottom was getting closer, and I could see some of the infrastructure at the bottom of the valley.

Suddenly I spotted a familiar couple ahead of me. An older man and a younger woman. It was the father-daughter duo who had swum in the river where I ate lunch! I snuck up behind them and whispered loudly, “Beware the piranhas!”  They turned, saw who it was, and burst out laughing.

Sources indicate that we started to chat and they were very interested and somewhat impressed at my having done the John Muir Trail. Falling into step with each other, the young woman talked about how she was planning to do the Mont Blanc Trail the next year.

According to recent reports, they asked a lot of questions about thru-hiking, and it was good for all of us. I induced them to pick up their pace a little, because I was still trying to make that YARTS departure and was not sure how long it might take to find the bus stop.

We were laughing and enjoying the easy downhill, when the trail suddenly ended at a tee. If there was a sign there, we didn’t see it, so we were puzzled as to whether to turn left or right. I stood in the middle of the intersection trying to figure it out, as they stood behind me, by the side of the trail we had come down. Just then….

Hi, I’m Papa George! In my 69 years I’ve done a lot of cool things – I’ve crossed the Atlantic in a 40-foot sailboat, bushwacked 100 miles across the north slope of the Alaska Range, hiked for 26 days in Western Nepal crossing five passes over 5,000 meters, and climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro, to name a few. It was my honor to serve my country as a diplomat around the world for 34 years. I have been active in retirement, and I hiked the Wonderland Trail in 2024 and the Long Trail in 2025. This year I'm trying... the John Muir Trail!

Industry News: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate prepares to vote this week on a bill aimed at easing America’s affordability crisis and fighting climate change that hunting and fishing groups worry will also erode many of the nation’s bedrock conservation laws.
  • The complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections.
  • In a recent development, BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the U.S. Senate prepares to vote this week on a bill aimed at easing America’s affordability crisis and fighting climate change that hunting and fishing groups worry will also erode many of the nation’s bedrock conservation laws.

The complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections. BAAJA also, however, ties jobs and household bills with curtailing public-lands protections. And in a twist that’s perplexing many conservation groups, the bill is co-sponsored by Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Mike Lee (R-Utah), two lawmakers known for being on nearly opposite ends of the public-lands spectrum.

In a recent development, BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. In practice, the legislation would raise the standard for whether projects approved by one administration can be revoked by a future administration.

Recent findings suggest that that means an industrial solar project permitted by one president, for example, could not be stymied by a future president intent on preventing renewables. It also speeds up permitting processes and cuts red tape for everything from energy projects to landscape-scale changes like prescribed fire.

But sportsmen and conservationists say the bill would not just expedite climate or environmentally friendly projects. BAAJA would also make it much harder — or potentially impossible — for an administration to overturn leases or approvals for projects as controversial as hyperscale data centers on public lands or mines in the same watersheds as sensitive wilderness areas. It’s a bill that prioritizes development, many observers say, at the cost of the very “red tape” that has been responsible for conserving many of the country’s most priceless fish, wildlife, and wild places.

Industry observers note that “I understand this is a major, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life. “Because when I say climate change is an existential threat, I mean it. And I will not let an opportunity to do something about it pass by.”.

Conservationists like Ingrid Lyons, executive director of Save the Boundary Waters, understand the need for stability around permitting development. The whiplash between issuing and revoking permits for public land development projects every time an administration changes has likely hurt the U.S.’s ability to move forward with important energy projects, including in renewables like wind and solar.

But she fears this bill could instead cement the creation of controversial projects like a copper-sulfide mine at the headwaters of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or a copper-molybdenum-gold mine in the salmon-rich waters of Alaska’s Bristol Bay. Permits for projects like these have been denied, among other issues, because of environmental risk. If permits are reissued in similar scenarios, legislation like BAAJA could prevent future administrations from stopping development in places that truly need protection.

In a recent development, “What about landscape certainty?” Lyons claims. “We’re overlooking in some ways the impact to communities that are relying on protection and not just projects.”.

It has been revealed that the conservation community has become increasingly vocal in its opposition to the bill since Heinrich and Lee partnered with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), and Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), to introduce the legislation in late September. Lee has a clear track record of supporting public land sales and undermining existing public-lands conservation, including 2025’s attempt to include federal land sales in the One Big Beautiful Bill.

In a recent development, A lengthy version of BAAJA is before the Senate as of Tuesday. The current bill includes a variety of red flags for hunters, anglers, tribes, endangered-species advocates, and other conservationists.

Some of the main points include:.

The Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership acknowledged the need for permit reform but said in a statement that “progress should not come at the expense of the conservation safeguards and public review that give hunters and anglers a voice in how our lands and waters are managed.”.

For Lyons, it comes down to the potential unintended consequences of sweeping legislation like BAAJA.

“We need to be exceptionally aware of the implications of this bill, which could be that a lot of these really beloved places could have projects many communities have worked really hard to oppose cemented into place.”.

Many in the conservation community were surprised by the bill’s sponsors, given Heinrich’s history as a sportsman and conservationist who regularly defends public lands and sensitive places, and Lee’s general position as a proponent of development and public-lands sell-off.

Industry observers note that but in Heinrich’s statement to Outdoor Life, he emphasizes the impact of climate change on our planet, including the places where people hunt, hike, bike and camp. Independent modeling, he said, predicts the bill will lead to a 20 percent reduction in power sector emissions, or the “equivalent to taking 39 coal plants offline for 10 years.”.

“You cannot protect a trout stream without paying attention to the warming temperatures and declining flows that threaten it,” he wrote. “You cannot protect wildlife habitat while ignoring the impacts of increasingly severe drought and wildfire. We need to reduce emissions, and that means getting more clean energy onto the grid.”.

In an Oct. 30 op-ed in the Albuquerque Journal, Heinrich explained how Fresh Mexico’s SunZia Wind and Transmission project took 17 years to permit and build.

In a recent development, he also pushed back on what he called misinformation about the bill, stating he doesn’t believe data centers should be on public land. The bill also requires large scale data center operators to pay the full cost of electricity consumed by the facility.

Sources indicate that the Izaak Walton League’s conservation director, Kate Miller, thinks each of the bill’s sponsors are acting in good faith and trying to do what is right for their constituents. Many projects, including those aimed at restoring forests and wildlife habitat, have been held up by permitting delays. Something like BAAJA could move those forward.

It has been revealed that but Miller would have liked to see these complications tackled individually instead of in a massive bill. And while she hopes that, if the bill passes, the administration will respect existing laws, the past two years has brought an onslaught of changes to most of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act.

“We want to make sure what comes out is not something that sacrifices those core protections that allow us to have healthy waters and habitats,” Miller states. “That we don’t sacrifice one for the other.”.

Read Next: Alaska Considers ‘Unprecedented’ Closure of Public Land to Hunting, Trapping Along Controversial Ambler Road.

Recent findings suggest that while the Senate is fast tracking the bill before the next Congress begins in January, it must move through the Senate and the House, and any changes be agreed upon by both chambers before the bill would land on President Trump’s desk. Meanwhile, both industry and conservation groups say they’re working to lobby lawmakers for changes and amendments. As a result, several conservation organizations declined to comment for this story.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An Idaho Fish and Game commissioner just made a deal to avoid poaching and trespassing charges related to an illegal elk hunt last season.
  • Industry observers note that on Nov.
  • His guilty pleas are for hunting without a tag and shooting across the road, according to local news outlets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Idaho Fish and Game commissioner just made a deal to avoid poaching and trespassing charges related to an illegal elk hunt last season.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 9 eastern Idaho’s representative, Brody Harshbarger, agreed to plead guilty to two of seven charges of wildlife violations in exchange for having the remaining charges dropped.

His guilty pleas are for hunting without a tag and shooting across the road, according to local news outlets. The dismissed charges include two for poaching, trespass, motorized aid and failure to retrieve game. Both of the killed animals were bull elk, one antlerless and the other a 6×6 which was on private property. Harshbarger was accompanied by another man, Eric Murphy, at the time.

Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, States He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

It has been revealed that “Neither Brody Harshbarger nor Eric Murphy called the landowners to request permission to retrieve the six-point bull and did not make a reasonable effort to retrieve the six-point bull,” according to investigation documents obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Neither individual had permission to be shooting onto the private property in violation of Idaho Code.”.

It has been revealed that harshbarger had already filled his elk tag the weekend before the two bulls were shot. His hometown, Ashton, is in the same county where the violations took place. That same county, Fremont, borders Yellowstone National Park and is in the region Harshbarger represents on the state’s seven-person commission. That commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists.

According to recent reports, each member of the commission, most often a resident hunter and/or fisherman, is appointed by the governor for a term of four years with a two-term maximum. The commission meets at least four times a year. Harshbarger hasn’t attended those meetings since his case opened after a tip received through the department’s Citizens Against Poaching in December. He hasn’t resigned and the Governor hasn’t dismissed him, but his profile has been removed from the commission’s website.

Recent findings suggest that “The Governor’s office is aware of Commissioner Harshbarger’s plea agreement,” Gov. Brad Little’s spokeswoman Emily Callihan told the Sun. “Gov. Little will be working with the Idaho Department of Fish and Game and stakeholders in the coming days to ensure the responsibilities of the position are fulfilled.”.

Harshbarger was appointed to the commission in 2024. His sentencing for illegal activities in 2025 is scheduled for Dec. 9. With the new plea deal and the number of charges reduced, the fine is expected to be $500 plus a one-year loss of hunting privileges.

Read Next: DNA Evidence Helps Convict Serial Poacher, Who Forfeited 2 Vehicles and Hunting Privileges for Life.

In a recent development, CAP received 1,596 calls about illegal wildlife-related activity in 2025, the highest on record since an annual total started rolling in 2019. A tip about a poached elk that leads to an arrest is worth $400. CAP rewarded tipsters more than $23,000 in 2025.
