📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

Recent findings suggest that the following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

In a recent development, “He was really lucky,” remarked Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

By the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

It has been revealed that as the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

Industry observers note that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

According to recent reports, the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Industry observers note that hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

Sources indicate that interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed initiative.

Industry observers note that despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

Industry observers note that at the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

#102266. Jeff Sturgis’ Secrets for Hunting Significant Whitetail Bucks

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1088 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Jeff Sturgis’ Secrets for Hunting Significant Whitetail Bucks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies.
  • Sources indicate that this summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks.
  • Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies. He’s honed these strategies through decades of hard hunting and consulting on his clients’ properties. He’s also tested them on his own 170-acre property in the bluff country of southern Minnesota (you can follow him on his YouTube channel, Whitetail Habitat Solutions).

Sources indicate that this summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks. In the video above, Sturgis runs through his five favorite setups and explains how he hunts them. Some of these setups take an immense amount of work and expense to develop. Others require minimal habitat work but a deep understanding of deer behavior.

Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.

Everyone talks about “buck bedding areas” but many hunters have only a vague understanding of them. The vital point, Sturgis claims, is that bucks do not like to bed near a lot of commotion, and that includes commotion from other deer. For example, does will often bed near major food sources. It’s convenient for them to get up from their bed and stroll right into a large food plot or ag field.

Mature bucks don’t like to bed around a mass of other deer. So buck beds will be found farther away from main food sources — even if there is prime bedding habitat right by those food sources. So just because you’re seeing a lot of does and young bucks in an area doesn’t mean it’s a good spot for mature bucks. In fact, it could mean the opposite.

Sources indicate that by crossing off areas where mature bucks won’t bed — again, areas with high pressure and activity — you can narrow down where they will bed. Sturgis isn’t afraid to hunt near buck bedding areas, but he does so sparingly. And when he does, he often takes his target buck.

Industry observers note that when you see deer consistently coming to a substantial food plot or agricultural field during daylight hours, it’s tempting to just hunt that major food source. Sturgis will hunt the big “holding plot” on his property, but only when he’s able to do so without spooking deer. He’s got a Redneck blind at the edge of the plot, which has an access route that is completely blocked by screening cover. He can get into and out of the blind with deer in the field — and never spook them. But that setup means he’s only able to hunt the big holding plot during gun season, even if there are target bucks hitting it during bow season.

According to recent reports, sturgis considers the holding plot the cornerstone of his entire property. So long as deer feel safe feeding there, he’s in the game. Even if he happens to bump a buck out of its bedding area, that deer is likely to switch bedding areas but still come to the holding plot to feed. This means that Sturgis can keep hunting that buck.

In a recent development, on the flipside, if he blows out the holding plot, it throws off deer behavior for the entire property, and that could be detrimental to his entire season. In some ways, he treats the holding plot like a sanctuary.

Sturgis has a ton of videos about how to set up and hunt waterholes. He creates his waterhole setups in the woods in traditional rut funnels. These waterholes give deer a reason to come within bow range and to stop there. Sturgis and his wife, Jen, have some of their best massive-buck hunts over waterholes.

These setups are relatively easy to implement, assuming you can get some kind of water tank into the woods where you hunt. They’re great places for all-day sits during the heart of the rut.

We all love to be in the woods before sunrise and to hear the telltale sound of a buck marching into range just after shooting light. But in some cases it’s impossible to hunt a spot first thing in the morning without spooking deer. These are often areas near field edges — deer are still in the fields feeding in the dark.

It has been revealed that in these scenarios Sturgis will simply enter the stand an hour or so after daylight when deer have left the field. This allows him to slip in undetected and have several hours of quality hunting before leaving again in the evening. These are usually high-probability sits during the rut.

According to recent reports, the main principle that Sturgis’ hunting strategy revolves around is to not overpressure mature deer. He wants big bucks to do their thing: rut, establish their dominance, and move around the habitat, during daylight hours. He lets his Tactacam trail cameras do the monitoring, and he picks his sits carefully. Of course we all love being in the woods and Sturgis does too. So he has stands that are very low impact for those times when he or someone in his family just wants to hunt — and you never know, a mature buck could stroll by any time.

But his approach is much more surgical when really targeting a specific deer.

According to recent reports, one of the many things I learned from Sturgis is that all of the knowledge (and much more) outlined above has been built into the Habitat IQ app. This app allows the user to draw in habitat features (like food sources, water, timber, and roads) into their own property. The program then uses a powerful algorithm, built off of Sturgis’ knowledge, to make habitat improvement suggestions and predict deer movement.

For example, if you don’t have any useful water sources on your property, the app will suggest adding some waterholes, and give you an idea about the best areas to place them.

Related: Here’s What Most Hunters Get Wrong About Whitetails, According to Jeff Sturgis.

The app is basically a digital version of Sturgis’ habitat/hunting consulting business. The more data you add into it, the better information you get back. I think this will be an incredibly powerful tool for anyone who is looking to implement the concepts that Sturgis has proven out over the course of 20-plus years of consulting on deer properties.

#102263. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1682 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • In a recent development, gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • The journey has not gone according to initiative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

In a recent development, gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to initiative. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

Recent findings suggest that but this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

Recent findings suggest that for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

It has been revealed that northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

According to recent reports, by the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

The route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line demonstrates the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

Industry observers note that I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

According to recent reports, safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

The kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

We have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

According to recent reports, the huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

Industry observers note that I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

You have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

It has been revealed that back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

In a recent development, the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

Sources indicate that the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

You can follow the expedition here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is swiftly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

It has been revealed that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

It has been revealed that on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Industry observers note that once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

It has been revealed that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

#102258. Tech Report: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Good Deer Hunting in Bad Weather

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2647 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Good Deer Hunting in Bad Weather

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A buck is not the only creature in the woods who gets into a “rut” during hunting season.
  • The point is, if you wish to improve your hunting success, you must be adaptable and let prevailing conditions, rather than past practices, determine your hunting methods.
  • Before devising hunting strategies based upon the weather, it will prove helpful to examine the effects of weather on deer behavior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A buck is not the only creature in the woods who gets into a “rut” during hunting season. Many hunters adopt a particular method of hunting and never consider changing it, even though the weather and, therefore, the hunting conditions change. For instance, many hunters automatically take to their tree stand and wait. To them, there is simply no other way to hunt. However, on very windy, cold days preceding and during the passage of a cold front, you can sit in a tree stand until you wear the brads off your britches and never see a deer. On the other hand, there are also hunters who would never climb a tree and who insist on still hunting. But on those days when the woods are extremely dry, you can walk to the next county without spotting anything.

The point is, if you wish to improve your hunting success, you must be adaptable and let prevailing conditions, rather than past practices, determine your hunting methods. While there is much to be noted for hunting hard and putting in a good effort, flexibility, rather than fortitude, is the key to good hunting on bad days.

Before devising hunting strategies based upon the weather, it will prove helpful to examine the effects of weather on deer behavior.

Sources indicate that as a rule, deer follow their normal routine of bedding, feeding, and moving throughout a wide range of climatic conditions. It is not unusual to see them feeding normally during rain or moving on breezy days. In general, scientists and observers agree about how deer act in relation to weather.

According to Al Berner, a biologist with the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, “Under typical rainy conditions, there is minimal effect on deer — they will continue to move about normally — but during a freezing rain, they will seek shelter.”.

He also reported that deer continue their normal movements during windy days, but are careful to move into the wind in order to more easily detect danger.

Dean Murphy, chief of the wildlife division of the Missouri Department of Conservation, mentioned deer increase their activity somewhat during normal rainy days. This is largely because light is reduced to a level nearer the diurnal range. The amount of daylight on overcast days closely resembles light in the early morning or late afternoon, which is when deer normally move.

Recent findings suggest that A study recently completed by Scott Hygnstrom, a graduate student at the University of Wisconsin at Stevens Point, revealed some interesting data on buck movements in relation to the wind. The study was conducted with the assistance of members of the Stump Sitters, an organization that studies deer behavior. The results of the study showed that, under perfectly calm wind conditions, there were fewer sightings of bucks than expected. However, under light wind conditions, there were more buck sightings than expected. As wind increased in velocity, buck sightings decreased proportionately.

Upon reflection, it seems reasonable that bucks would be more active in a light wind. The wind would make it possible for them to detect danger more easily by catching the scent. At the same time, their ability to hear would not be as diminished as it would be in a strong wind.

Francis X. Leuth, formerly a biologist with the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, discovered that the same holds true for whitetails in the Southern United States. Deer continue normal movements in rain and wind unless it becomes very strong or very cold. During such times, deer will hold in cover — sometimes for as long as several days.

All researchers agreed that deer tend to hold up during very heavy weather, whether it be cold rain, wind, sleet, or snow. Most of them also reported increased movement 12 to 36 hours before an advancing front and immediately after its passage.

These authorities also agreed on another point: If hunters continued to hunt during bad weather instead of looking for a warm dry place to wait it out, they would be much more successful.

Before examining various weather conditions and the hunting methods best suited to coping with them, it is crucial to define the three types of hunting that will be recommended.

The first of these, stand hunting, involves taking a position — either up in a tree or in ground cover — and watching one area for the duration of the hunt. While stand hunting has many advantages, its primary disadvantage is that you are limited in the territory that you can cover. If deer are not moving in the area that you are watching, the hunt is over!

Recent findings suggest that walk-and-stand hunting means finding concealment on the ground and watching an area for a period of time, then moving on to a new area. The idea is to watch different kinds of areas to determine where the deer are located. It is somewhat like a bass fisherman trying to establish a pattern by fishing in different kinds of structure, depths, and locations.

Stillhunting involves intermittently moving and stopping in a slow, deliberate pattern as you move through the woods. It offers you the opportunity to cover more territory, but it also provides deer with an opportunity to spot you.

According to recent reports, some of the conditions that indicate a need to change hunting routines are sudden changes in the weather, days of heavy rain, windy days, and extremely dry conditions. Let’s look at them in detail and see which hunting method best fits each one.

A sudden change in the weather is usually associated with an approaching low-pressure system. For some reason that is not fully understood, all wildlife seem to be more active under these conditions. It is not known for certain whether they know that bad weather is coming and are moving to areas that offer better protection, or if they are eating an extra portion to hold them over for a while. For these reasons, or for some other unexplained reason, their movements increase during these few short hours.

Regardless of the reasons, this type of behavior carries certain implications for hunting techniques. During an approaching front, the walk-and-stand hunter may have a slight advantage. The stand hunter usually places his stand along known trails leading to and from feeding and bedding areas. He also tends to hunt in the morning and the afternoon in order to take advantage of the early/late movement pattern. Because of frequent variations in their movement patterns during an approaching front, deer may not follow their established routines, thus lessening the chance that one will pass by when the stand hunter expects.

The stillhunter is also at a disadvantage because, although the deer are more active, they are also more alert. Because they are more exposed to danger, they exercise greater caution.

Industry observers note that walk-and-stand hunting offers the best combination of stand and stalk hunting, especially if you stay in the woods all day. The best pattern is to pick a location that offers an open area — not necessarily an open field — and to watch for movement near the edges of cover. For instance, if you can find an open hardwood hollow bordered by pine thickets or honeysuckle, you may find some crossing action or movement along the borders of the thick cover.

After watching an area for an hour or so, move to another location and repeat the pattern. This allows you to cover a lot of territory during a day, and you are likely to find an area in which the deer are moving.

It has been revealed that the most uncomfortable condition to hunt under is rain. If you are going to hunt in the rain, stillhunting offers some advantages. First, you can move very quietly when the ground is wet. Secondly, you can cover more territory. This is often required during rain because you have to go to the deer if they are not moving.

Recent findings suggest that during periods of light rain, the deer’s behavior is hardly affected at all and there would be little need to change a preferred method of hunting under these conditions. However, if you are not skilled at still hunting and wish to learn more about it, this would be an ideal time to give it a try.

Sources indicate that if you are not an experienced stillhunter, it is a very awkward and difficult method to develop confidence in. You feel exposed and think that everything in the woods is hiding and watching you. In turn, the temptation is to try to hide behind trees, rocks, and bushes. The problem is that you always see a better place in front of you and you keep moving from one hiding place to another. Soon, you have gone through the area that you were supposed to be hunting and have come out convinced either that nothing was there or that stillhunting is a waste of time. The problem is, you were concentrating on hiding instead of on hunting.

Related: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

A few points may prove helpful in learning this highly productive method of hunting. First, move as slowly as possible. Deer see movement more easily than they recognize objects. Second, when you stop, kneel down to blend into the ground cover or lean against a tree so that you are not silhouetted. And third, move less and look more. Study every area of cover and use binoculars! Look for parts of a deer such as an ear, a leg, and especially for the horizontal lines of a back or a belly among the vertical lines of trees or bushes. Many hunters think that binoculars are used primarily to see great distances, but their best use is to find small pieces of a deer in thick cover.

Probably the only thing worse than hunting in the rain is hunting when the woods are bone dry. It is more comfortable to the hunter, but it means more difficult hunting. Every movement and crunch of leaves is a signal to the deer to clear out.

Recent findings suggest that stillhunting and walk-and-stand hunting are difficult, if not impossible, during dry weather, leaving stand hunting as the most logical choice. You may want to choose a ground blind for convenience’s sake but, where it is legal, hunting from a stand in a tree enlarges the area that you can hunt effectively.

Even with the advantage of being able to see better from a tree stand, remember that you cannot see everything at all times. You can only see about one-third of the area at any time and many opportunities for a shot can be missed if you are not alert.

Sources indicate that if you want to prove this to yourself, think about how many times you have suddenly noticed a deer standing in the open, 15 or 20 yards from the nearest cover. It did not simply appear on that spot. The deer walked there while you were looking somewhere else. It hurts to think how many go by unnoticed.

The principal way in which dry weather helps the stand hunter is that it cuts down on the area that you have to watch. You patrol the area with both your eyes and your ears. A deer can move more quietly than you can but, when it is dry, even deer will give away their position. On windy days or when the woods are wet, however, deer can slip by without a sound.

Industry observers note that one effective technique is to locate your stand on the edge of a field or an open woodland area. You can then hunt the open area with your eyes and the thick woods with your ears, thus covering your hunting area more thoroughly.

If it is not too wet or too dry, it can always be too windy. Wind has probably saved hunters more ammunition than any other weather condition. I’m not referring to those days when there is a steady breeze blowing — this can be beneficial to the hunter — but rather to those days when it is bitter cold and the wind seems to come from all directions at the same time. On these days, deer will either hold in thick cover and not expose themselves or they will pick up your scent and slip away without your ever knowing that they were there.

Using a buddy system to move deer into the open offers an opportunity to get a shot at a good buck on such days, but the plan must be carefully thought out in advance. Pre-planning not only places hunters in the most opportune positions to get the best shot, but also provides a safety measure in that they know where not to shoot.

Sources indicate that for the purpose of illustration, consider a hunting situation in an agricultural area with woods dispersed between fields. The driver should start on the downwind side of the thickest cover in the hope of moving the deer down the hollow into more open areas or across the field into the adjoining woods. If there are fingers of the land protruding out into the fields, they provide natural escape routes. Bucks in particular will cross an open area at its narrowest point.

Hunters should position themselves to cover these routes, but it is better if they take a stand across the field in the adjacent woods, rather than in the same area of woods.

Recent findings suggest that contrary to appearances, deer do not leave the state when disturbed. They leave the area of disturbance quickly, but soon resume their normal activity at a much slower pace.

When a deer is jumped and makes its escape across an open area, it will likely slow down once it is out of the immediate area of danger. Often, if you take a stand along an escape route away from the jump area, this will mean a standing or walking shot rather than a quick glimpse of a white flag. Contrary to appearances, deer do not leave the state when disturbed. They leave the area of disturbance swiftly, but soon resume their normal activity at a much slower pace. Hunters should be stationed at other escape points and farther down the hollow in case a jumped deer chooses to move on down the wood line rather than cross the open field.

Recent findings suggest that when attempting to move deer out of cover, it is better to stop occasionally than to walk continuously. Often, a deer will watch from cover and let a hunter walk on by. If you have ever observed deer while driving, you may have seen a similar reaction. If you keep moving, they stand and watch but, if you stop, they move out. The same thing is often true of a continuously moving versus a moving-and-stopping technique of hunting.

Sources indicate that A buddy system of moving deer can be devised for any type of terrain you hunt. The notable points to remember are to use the system in an area that everyone is familiar with, to identify the stand placements carefully and, for safety’s sake, to coordinate the time and the direction of movements of each person.

According to recent reports, occasionally, even for those of us who are willing to modify our hunting techniques and to learn latest ways to hunt on bad days, there are those times when it is neither too wet, too dry, nor too windy. And on those days, even if you don’t see a deer, you can always think, “What a great day to be hunting!”.

This story, “Good Deer Hunting On Bad Days,” appeared in the April 1985 matter of Outdoor Life.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • According to recent reports, A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • It has been revealed that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

According to recent reports, A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

It has been revealed that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Industry observers note that eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

Industry observers note that A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He stated climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • It has been revealed that if you head north and east out of Salt Lake City toward the Wyoming state line you end up in some of the most stunning country in the United States.
  • Industry observers note that but once you get past the view from the winding highways that snake through this land and gain some elevation on the dirt roads that take you back to more remote areas, you’ll notice something else.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

It has been revealed that if you head north and east out of Salt Lake City toward the Wyoming state line you end up in some of the most stunning country in the United States. At first glance, it looks like a semi-arid range of mountains with the exposed shelves of red rock, patches of sage, and grassy benches typical of the Intermountain West at this latitude.

Industry observers note that but once you get past the view from the winding highways that snake through this land and gain some elevation on the dirt roads that take you back to more remote areas, you’ll notice something else. These mountains give birth to a surprising number of springs, providing water that ends up supporting a vast amount of life.

The wet country reveals itself in the stands of aspen that grow thick in places you wouldn’t expect, with waist-high grass that contrasts with the blanket of drought-resistant scrub oak that covers much of the terrain.

According to recent reports, this almost contradictory mix of moisture, cover, food, and remoteness provides a recipe for great elk and mule deer, and is the reason I’ll return to this country whenever I can, as happened a few weeks ago this fall. I was there on an invitation from Winchester Ammunition to try its newest offering, Supreme Long Range, on my favorite North American game.

Industry observers note that there are many reasons mule deer have such a strong claim on my psyche. I love the wild places they call home. The hours spent glassing them is about the most rewarding way to pass time. And I find it infinitely fascinating to watch and study their behavior.

You see, mule deer are a study in contradiction, too. Are their numbers in decline? In many places, without a doubt. They’ve certainly struggled to maintain their hold in much of their traditional range. Housing and energy development disrupt their winter grounds and migration routes. Diseases like CWD have taken their toll, especially with older bucks. We know that blossoming herds of elk and whitetails can outcompete mulies for food and water, putting more pressure on their numbers.

But they are also resilient and, in some areas, thrive. Good numbers of mule deer live in suburban areas throughout the mountain west. And you can find them in some of the most inhospitable desert regions of North America, and tucked away in other unlikely places.

Though they can seem more docile than their high-strung white-tailed cousins, I have witnessed mule deer put on incredible displays of strength, aggression, and John-Wick-caliber willpower — another contradiction.

Recent findings suggest that years ago in Colorado, I watched a hunter fail to follow up his shot on a mule deer. The high-shoulder shot dropped the buck where it stood, knocking it senseless. The hunter started celebrating, thinking he had killed it, and when the deer regained its feet the hunter wasn’t ready — and the buck disappeared into the alders. I helped track the deer for several hours through the snow, following a substantial blood trail. We kept going as long as we could after dark but eventually had to call it quits.

Recent findings suggest that the hunter left for the airport and I kept looking for the deer with my good friend Cody while trying to fill my own tag. Two days later, Cody and I spotted the buck tending his does, despite the grievous wound in his upper chest and one ruined leg. He was 500 yards away, skylined on the ridge, and I couldn’t get a shot off before he fled over the mountain.

Sources indicate that there was no doubt in my mind the buck was going to die from that injury, but procreation was his sole preoccupation. Despite the obvious pain, and the imminent certainty of death, he would not be deterred.

That buck spurned death, but I’ve also seen mule deer inflict it. I was hunting in southeast Montana a few years back in mid-November when the rut was in full swing. Bucks were bird-dogging does, scent-checking the ladies, cruising in search of mates, and squaring up against potential rivals.

Usually when two bucks face off they will posture a bit and, after sizing each other up, one will back off before things get too heated. Sometimes they will fight — those antlers aren’t just for decoration — and the vanquished male will make his excuses to be elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that in this case, the smaller of the deer lost his footing during the scuffle and fell back, rolling on his side. The larger buck lowered his head and drove his antlers into the other’s exposed belly.

The deer on his side flailed his legs in a desperate attempt to get up and escape, but through my binocular I could see the spreading circle of red in the snow as the dominant buck continued the savage attack, never letting up.

After several minutes — it felt like an eternity from my vantage — the buck’s fury was spent and he lifted his head and walked off as the other deer lay still, surrounded by his own gore.

I relate this because it is one thing to enjoy hunting, which I do, but it is another to, on occasion, experience the wild at its most raw and profound.

So, when I got this latest opportunity to test my legs and lungs in the high-country in Utah, I had hopes of encountering a mature buck, and perhaps more.

Industry observers note that I was joined on the trip by Kyle Masinelli, the vice president of manufacturing operations at Winchester Ammunition, and a friend and work colleague of mine, Ed Friedman, the editor-in-chief of American Rifleman. Kyle was one of the architects of Winchester Supreme Long Range and a great source of information about it.

As the name implies, Supreme Long Range (SLR for short) is geared toward substantial-game hunting where longer shots might be in the offing, which is often the case when mule deer hunting. This newly introduced ammo uses what Winchester calls their “BC Max” bullet, which is a heavy-for-caliber cup-and-core design with an oversized polymer tip to initiate rapid expansion.

Over the summer, I shot several boxes of this new ammunition, chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor, with excellent results in terms of its precision and consistency.

It has been revealed that I gathered 20 shots of data with three different rifles, shooting four 5-shot groups with each. Those twelve 5-shot groups ranged in size from .53 inches to 1.10 inches. The overall average group size was .818 inches.

In a curious coincidence, the mean radius value for each of the three rifles was .32 inches, which is very good for hunting ammunition.

The three rifles I used to gather the data were Proof’s MTR Elevation FDX, which won an Editor’s Choice for best hunting rifle of the year; Seekins Precision’s latest PH3 NRL Hunter, which won an Editor’s Choice for best crossover rifle; and a Seekins Precision SIC Short Action, which won’t be officially debuted until early 2027.

According to recent reports, for the hunt itself, I went a different route, taking a Winchester XPR chambered in 6.8 Western. The XPR has been a perennial choice of ours for an entry-level hunting rifle. It is a no-frills bolt-action that delivers good performance. In its most basic black synthetic stock trim it can be had for less than $600 new.

It has been revealed that while I’ve shot plenty of XPRs over the years, I hadn’t had as much time with the 6.8 Western. I shot this souped-up .270 Winchester a bit when it was first rolled out in 2021, but had never done a deep dive on the cartridge or taken it hunting.

I didn’t have as much trigger time with the XPR and the ammunition as I would have liked before rolling into camp, but I did establish a solid zero prior to making the drive from Montana to Utah and knew that the 175-grain 6.8mm SLR bullets were exiting my 22-inch barrel right at 2,700 fps.

It has been revealed that we were hunting with the R&K Hunting Tech giant, which has a base camp in Coalville, Utah, and I confirmed my dope on targets they had there. With three shots, I checked my point of impact at 200, 500, and 700 yards, the bullets ringing the center of the steel each time.

Our hunting camp was another hour’s drive into the mountains, most of it off-road, and much of it pitted with craters like small bomb impacts.

But the camp itself was an alpine Shangri-La. The main lodge was a cozy wood structure where the hunters stayed, with a series of small cabins for the guides, and other out buildings, all overlooking a post-card scene of a small lake surrounded by golden-leafed quakies and distant mountains.

Those mountains were where we hunted.

Kyle and I spent the first day with our guides, two young brothers named Keston and Kandon Mosher, glassing the heights. In the afternoon, we spotted two excellent bucks engaged in pre-rut posturing.

Sources indicate that from nearly a mile away we watched the bucks through our optics. One of the bucks appeared to have a larger, darker body and a heavier rack. The other buck was mature as well, seemingly younger, but with larger antlers. Both were stunning.

We watched them circle each other a bit in a small clearing between stands of alders. We needed to move promptly, because the cover around them was thick, it was getting late, and we were losing light.

We grabbed our packs and guns and hoofed up the mountain as fast as we could. It took about half an hour of hard climbing to get to the knob we wanted to set up on. That put us within 800 yards of where we’d last seen the deer.

According to recent reports, assuming we spotted them again, we’d make a final plan. But that didn’t happen. We glassed the ridge until dark. We could see many of the other deer we’d been watching, but the bucks had vanished. As has happened to me so many times while going after substantial mule deer, they’d given us the slip.

Recent findings suggest that we returned to the base of that mountain ahead of sunrise, peering into the cover as the light came up. With each passing minute, we took in more ground.

In a recent development, the mountain was actually a long, fairly flat ridge running north to south that topped out at 9,200 feet, and encompassed five separate large drainages. From end-to-end it spanned over three miles. The middle section seemed to hold the most animals, but we frequently spotted elk and deer at the northern and southern edges too.

Recent findings suggest that early on, Keston caught a flash of antler in an alder thicket not far from the top of the ridge. We all trained our optics on the spot and after a bit the lighter-colored buck stepped into the open. We easily identified him based on his coloration and the picture-perfect four-point frame he carried above his head.

He was feeding on his own about 350 yards from where we’d seen him the previous afternoon. About 30 yards below him was a doe and two fawns, also munching on grass. The other big buck was nowhere to be seen.

Recent findings suggest that there was no way to get to him from below. Even if we could approach from that direction without busting him he’d be out of sight until we stepped into the same clearing. That clearly wouldn’t work. Plus it would take well over an hour and a half to hike up there at which point he’d certainly be gone even if we were as stealthy as ninjas.

Recent findings suggest that instead, we hiked back down to our side-by-side and took a long looping route to the top of the ridge. From this new vantage, the terrain presented more of a challenge than I would have guessed. Looking down, I could see benches and pockets of cover that were invisible from lower down. This included small natural ponds and abundant feed. An animal could move through that all day and never reveal itself to a hunter glassing from below.

It has been revealed that we parked well away from where we saw the buck last and snuck along the spine until we were above his feeding spot. We crept toward the edge and peered down the slope.

At this point the wind shifted so it was coming from directly behind us. We saw the doe and her fawns scoot out of the pocket, having clearly caught our scent.

But the buck should have been between us and them, and if he followed a similar escape route, I would get a shot. We held tight for a quarter hour but saw no sign of him. He’d obviously slipped away in a safer, more hidden direction.

Sources indicate that I wasn’t surprised. Mule deer get a bad rap for acting dumb during the rut. And it’s true that some bucks seem to throw caution to the wind when love is in the air. But in my experience I’ve seen more evidence of their clever and well-honed survival instincts preserving them from eager hunters, especially when it comes to truly mature bucks.

That afternoon we returned to the base of the ridge. We set up beneath the knob from the previous night because we didn’t want to overcommit and potentially bust the bucks in case they had moved lower down the mountain.

It has been revealed that it wasn’t long before we spotted a latest buck working its way down a drainage to our right. He was a handsome 4×4 with eyeguards, and Kyle wanted to take him.

He set his .300 Win. Mag. in a tripod and shot the buck at 350 yards from a kneeling position. The bullet was perfectly placed and the buck ran a few steps and tumbled over. Kyle, Keston, and Kandon (which sounds not unlike a law firm) took off to recover the buck while I stayed behind to keep glassing.

In a recent development, by the time Keston returned we had about an hour left of shooting light. As luck would have it, we caught sight of the light-colored deer trying to sneak off to the south.

With the pressure we’d applied to the north half of the ridge that morning and afternoon (Kyle’s deer was in the same drainage as the bench where we spotted the buck after first light) I wasn’t surprised to see the older deer trying to put some distance between us and him.

Industry observers note that once again it was a race against the falling light. Keston and I took off up the mountain to get within range before dark.

According to recent reports, we hiked for 20 minutes to an exposed point that gave us a good view. Keston found the deer again, walking to our left and down toward a thick stand of aspen in a steep draw, where he was about to disappear.

I ranged the deer at 616 yards and got prone, deploying my bipod and setting the butt of the XPR on my shooting bag. The wind, which had been howling earlier in the day, was calming down, but still needed to be accounted for.

I dialed elevation into my scope, held left .4 mil for the wind, and broke the shot. The deer dropped as if poleaxed, kicked a bit, and then lay still. I watched him through my scope with a fresh round chambered until I was sure he was dead.

Sources indicate that by the time we got to the vicinity of the deer it was pitch black. Finding an animal under these conditions can be difficult. And while technology is often a two-edged affairm in this case it was a godsend.

According to recent reports, for the last year, I’ve been using Leupold’s BX-6 rangefinding binocular in shooting competitions and while hunting. I won’t go into all its virtues here, but one feature that’s a game changer is its ability to range a spot and have it drop a pin into a map, like onX Hunt.

That pin led us right to the buck, saving us who knows how much time stumbling around the dark.

Recent findings suggest that every hunting bullet has the same end goal, which is to inflict massive tissue damage so that the animal rapidly bleeds out, shutting the central nervous system down. (Alternatively, a bullet can strike the CNS directly, with a brain or spinal shot, killing the animal that way.).

In a recent development, how a bullet accomplishes this depends heavily on its construction. Bonded bullets, for instance, are meant to mushroom to a degree, while retaining weight and penetrating deeply.

Recent findings suggest that the BC Max bullet takes a different approach. The large polymer tip on the projectile initiated quick and violent bullet upset. The entrance hole, in the upper portion of the chest, was about two inches across and busted two ribs on the way in.

I could tell the bullet fragmented significantly based on three things: that large entrance wound, the massive tissue damage observed on the deer’s lungs, and the fact that the bullet didn’t penetrate the off side of the ribcage.

We quartered the deer and took backstraps, loins, and neck meat without gutting it, so I didn’t try to recover what was left of the bullet, though I doubt it would have been much.

It has been revealed that of all the big mule deer I’ve shot over my career, this one comes closest to the Platonic ideal. He’s a large, clean four-point, with deep, nearly identical, forks front and back, has a tall boxy frame, carries good mass throughout his rack, and has nice eye guards to boot. If one were to draw an idealized symmetrical mule deer, it would look a lot like this one.

I never take an animal like this for granted. He was a wily deer and had given us the slip a couple times already, and was about to make it a third. And, of course, there was his older cousin, that darker, heavier brute, who only indicated himself once.

According to recent reports, we were the last deer hunters on that mountain this season. And my fingers are crossed that the other substantial buck, and his kin, make it through the winter.

I don’t say that because I expect to hunt that spot again. There’s very little chance that will happen. But I do hope some other hunter, who loves these animals the way I do, at least gets to encounter that buck and possibly take him home.

Read Next: Why Mule Deer (Not Whitetails) Are North America’s Greatest Game Animal.

That’s the shared dream all avid mule deer hunters have, and is what draws us to the mountains each fall in pursuit of America’s most interesting, complicated, and magnificent species of game.

  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
  • The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a newly introduced attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

The fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

Industry observers note that on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.
